Akinola Davies Jr. with his BAFTA trophy for My Father’s Shadow. Photo Credit: Akinola Davies Jr./Instagram Kemi Adetiba Before crossing into cinema and streaming, Kemi Adetiba built a reputation directing memorable music videos for artists including Wizkid , Tiwa Savage , Olamide , and Banky W . On the big screen, she shattered box-office records with The Wedding Party and followed up with the crime drama King of Boys , its sequel King of Boys: The Return of the King , and the series To Kill a Monkey . Her sharp pacing, bold casting, and distinct visual style have kept her in the spotlight across platforms such as The Headies, the City People Entertainment Awards, and the AMVCAs. Kemi Adetiba and Bucci Franklin on the set of To Kill a Monkey. Photo Credit: Kemi Adetiba/Instagram Daniel Etim Effiong Many movie lovers know Daniel Etim Effiong first as a familiar leading man across Nollywood films and streaming hits, yet his work behind the camera is just as central to his career. Having studied filmmaking at AFDA in South Africa and gained experience on shorts and television episodes, he stepped into feature directing with the thriller The Herd . That debut brought him Best Director and Best Debut Feature Film by a Director nominations at the 2026 Africa Movie Academy Awards, while The Herd collected three AMAA trophies and earned nine AMVCA nominations, including Best Director. Daniel Etim Effiong on the set of The Herd which leads the 12th AMVCA nominations with 9 nods including Best Director. Dammy Twitch Known for years for directing visually bold music videos for stars like Davido , Burna Boy , and Omah Lay , Dammy Twitch ( Apampa Oluwadamilola Owolabi ) made his feature film directing debut in May 2026 with the romantic comedy Call of My Life . Led by Uzoamaka Power and Andrew Yaw Bunting alongside Zubby Michael , Beverly Osu , Nkem Owoh , Patience Ozokwor , and Broda Shaggi , the film crossed ₦900 million at the Nigerian box office to become one of the highest-grossing Nollywood releases of 2026, while also winning the Favourite Feature Narrative Audience Award at the 2026 BlackStar Film Festival. Bringing his instincts for framing, colour, and pacing from music visuals into narrative cinema, he has quickly become a fresh voice movie fans are keeping a close eye on. Dammy Twitch on the set of Call of My Life. item.title: Danny Kelly loved football and never forgot the absurdity of earning a living talking about it | Max Rushden
item.description: The journalist and broadcaster who died last week aged 69 knew the enduring power of radio, even as the landscape changed so quickly It’s injury time at the Emirates on the 29 October 2008, Arsenal are 4-3 up against Spurs. Tom Huddlestone cushions a ball to Luka Modric, whose strike takes a deflection. It loops over Manuel Almunia and on to the post into the path of Aaron Lennon, who prods it home and starts skipping towards the Spurs fans before diving on to the ground and being enveloped by Modric, Benoît Assou-Ekotto, Darren Bent and a couple of pitch-invading fans. Pandemonium, for once, seems the apt way to describe it. But the real entertainment is happening in a radio studio at 18 Hatfields, London SE1; the old home of TalkSport. As the goal goes in, a guttural voice makes an indecipherable but very loud noise. It’s hard to transcribe – perhaps “ERRRRRAAAARRRGGHH”, or maybe “OOEEERRAAGGH”. Continue reading...

item.title: Super Eagles must improve or miss 2027 AFCON – Jo Bonfere
item.description: Former Super Eagles coach, Jo Bonfrere, has warned that Nigeria could miss out on the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations if the team fails to improve its performance in the remaining qualifying matches. Bonfrere gave the warning following Nigeria’s goalless draw against Tanzania’s Taifa Stars in Zanzibar on Tuesday, a result he described as a setback to the country’s qualification campaign. The result left the three-time African champions second in Group L with seven points from four matches, three points behind leaders Guinea-Bissau, who defeated Madagascar 2-0 in Bissau. With only group winners guaranteed qualification for the tournament, the former coach said Nigeria must win their remaining fixtures to avoid putting their AFCON hopes in jeopardy. Speaking to Complete Sports, Bonfrere said the Super Eagles missed an opportunity to close the gap on Guinea-Bissau with a victory in Zanzibar. “It’s a poor result for the Super Eagles,” he said. “The Super Eagles should have done better. A win would have bridged the gap with Guinea-Bissau. But with this result, they will have to work hard in their two remaining games or risk seeing their 2027 AFCON ambition fade,” the 80-year-old said. Bonfrere, who led Nigeria’s U-23 team to football gold at the 1996 Olympic Games in Atlanta, Georgia, also expressed concern over the team’s scoring record in the qualifiers. Nigeria have scored five goals and conceded the same number in four Group L matches, a record the Dutch tactician said was below expectations, considering the quality of players available to the country. He argued that the Super Eagles should be scoring more goals, given that several members of the squad feature for top European clubs. “You score goals, you win games. If you don’t score, you don’t win. The Super Eagles have good players in top European teams. They have more experience than any other team in Africa. So, they must score goals,” he said. Comparing Nigeria’s performance with that of Guinea-Bissau, Bonfrere noted that the group leaders had scored eight goals and conceded just one in their four matches. “You said Guinea-Bissau have scored eight goals and conceded one. That’s good for them. That’s what the Super Eagles should be doing, and even more, because Nigeria have quality players,” he added. Nigeria will return to action in March 2027 when they travel to face Madagascar in their Matchday Five encounter, while Guinea-Bissau host Tanzania. The Super Eagles will then conclude their qualifying campaign against Guinea-Bissau at the Godswill Akpabio International Stadium, Uyo, on March 28. Both fixtures are crucial to Nigeria’s chances of securing a place at the 2027 AFCON. The post Super Eagles must improve or miss 2027 AFCON – Jo Bonfere appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Microsoft To Do will soon become Microsoft Done
item.description: Microsoft has slipped some bad news into this week's Ignite AI puffery: the To Do apps are retiring on June 30, 2027, ending a journey that began with its acquisition of Wunderlist more than a decade ago. The confirmation came in an announcement about unified tasks and plans for Copilot and Microsoft 365. Until now, there was To Do or Planner (in basic or premium guise). The idea is "a single system for tracking your work as an individual, as a team, and as an organization." To Do contributes features to that future, but its apps don't get to join it. The problem is that Planner doesn't do everything To Do does. Microsoft would like users to migrate to Planner but, by the company's own admission , there are plenty of gaps. No native Windows or Mac desktop apps are planned to replace To Do; file attachments aren't supported on tasks in the Planner private plan, and there's no equivalent to To Do list groups in Planner. "Equivalent To Do printing and email-list capabilities are not currently planned for the replacement experience," and so on. Existing To Do tasks and lists won't migrate to Planner either. They'll remain accessible through Planner until June 30, 2027, but that access ends with the apps. Microsoft says the date does not itself trigger deletion of the underlying data. Personal Microsoft account holders are left in an even worse state: Planner isn't available to them, including Microsoft 365 Personal and Family subscribers. Microsoft's advice is to choose another task-management app and prepare to export their data. Export instructions are still to come, and exporting won't necessarily produce something another app can import. Very much a case of "don't let the door hit you on the way out." Unifying tasks and plans is a good idea – the current situation does create confusion, as Microsoft acknowledged. However, taking an axe to To Do, which was developed to be a successor to Wunderlist ( acquired in 2015 for a figure between $100 million and $200 million, an early action under Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella), seems extreme. Microsoft calls the replacement "a unified platform for people and agents across Microsoft 365" and stated: "This unified platform makes accessing Planner through Copilot, Cowork and Autopilot easier." Some users responding to the announcement were unimpressed, with one declaring "What a mess," and another asking if To Do might be spun off into an open source project: "Not everything needs to be put into an AI/Copilot agent." Indeed, it doesn't. But a useful service that doesn't ram Copilot and AI integration down customers' throats at every opportunity? That would never do. The message for To Do users appears to be: Get with the Plan(ner) or just get out. ®

item.description: PRESS REVIEW – Thursday, November 19: An historic trilateral summit takes place in Shenzhen between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin. item.title: Nigeria: States set to get their own police forces
item.description: Nigeria has moved a step closer to letting its 36 states set up their own police forces. The National Assembly has sent a constitutional amendment bill to the president, as authorities seek state-run police to complement the federal force amid growing insecurity. Many states currently fund vigilante groups to fight armed groups like Boko Haram, but these groups are poorly trained and ill-equipped for the task. FRANCE 24's correspondent has the latest.

item.title: Unionism not a licence for irresponsibility, Wike’s aide slams UniAbuja staff
item.description: …Says varsity used only 1,426.67 hectares in 38 yrs By Omeiza Ajayi ABUJA: Lere Olayinka, Senior Special Assistant on Public Communications and Social Media to the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory FCT, Nyesom Wike, has told staff of the University of Abuja that “unionism and activism should not be a licence for reckless advertisement of irresponsible behaviour” as they agitate over the reduction of the institution’s land from 11,824.04 hectares to 4,685 hectares. In a statement on Thursday in Abuja, Olayinka described the utterances of the union leaders, especially the chairman of the Academic Staff Union of Universities ASUU at the university, Professor Sylvanus Ugoh, as unbecoming of people operating in an academic environment. Olayinka said after existing for 38 years, the university had used a fraction of its land. “Most importantly, after existing for 38 years, UNIABUJA has only utilized 1,426.67 hectares of land, with 49.56 hectares used for staff quarters. What then is the need for over 11,000 hectares of land when less than 1,500 hectares was utilized in 38 years?” he asked. He dismissed the claim by the Joint Action Committee (JAC), which is seeking a reversal of the reduction, that the Minister forged the 2016 report of the Joint Committee of the Federal Capital Territory Administration (FCTA) and UNIABUJA on Land and Sundry Issues. The committee was set up by the then FCT Minister, Mohamed Musa Bello. Olayinka called the allegation recklessness and irresponsibility taken too far. “It is therefore strange that supposed academia will hide under an unknown Joint Action Committee to insult the person of the FCT Minister and accuse him of forging official documents of the government arising from a committee duly set up by his predecessor,” he said. He added that apart from the 2016 committee, another one was set up on December 17, 2020, following the university management’s visit to the FCT Minister on October 13, 2020. According to him, part of the recommendations of the December 2020 committee read: “Based on the recommended size of 100Ha for a University Campus stipulated by the National University Commission and considering that the University has held the title of about 11,608.33Ha for over thirty (30) years, a total of about 1,922.66Ha should be left to the University while the remaining part of the land should be designed and detailed by URP (Urban and Regional Planning) Department for compatible land use like Institution and Research Districts.” The recommendation went on: “This will solve the issues of continuous and unabated village expansion which will save the FCTA the unending trouble of village encroachments and the cost of removing them.” Olayinka said the issues the university presented to the 2016 committee included the issuance of Certificate of Occupancy for its main and mini campuses and its properties in Kado and Jahi districts. item.content:encoded: …Says varsity used only 1,426.67 hectares in 38 yrs By Omeiza Ajayi ABUJA: Lere Olayinka, Senior Special Assistant on Public Communications and Social Media to the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory FCT, Nyesom Wike, has told staff of the University of Abuja that “unionism and activism should not be a licence for reckless advertisement of irresponsible behaviour” as they agitate over the reduction of the institution’s land from 11,824.04 hectares to 4,685 hectares. In a statement on Thursday in Abuja, Olayinka described the utterances of the union leaders, especially the chairman of the Academic Staff Union of Universities ASUU at the university, Professor Sylvanus Ugoh, as unbecoming of people operating in an academic environment. Olayinka said after existing for 38 years, the university had used a fraction of its land. “Most importantly, after existing for 38 years, UNIABUJA has only utilized 1,426.67 hectares of land, with 49.56 hectares used for staff quarters. What then is the need for over 11,000 hectares of land when less than 1,500 hectares was utilized in 38 years?” he asked. He dismissed the claim by the Joint Action Committee (JAC), which is seeking a reversal of the reduction, that the Minister forged the 2016 report of the Joint Committee of the Federal Capital Territory Administration (FCTA) and UNIABUJA on Land and Sundry Issues. The committee was set up by the then FCT Minister, Mohamed Musa Bello. Olayinka called the allegation recklessness and irresponsibility taken too far. “It is therefore strange that supposed academia will hide under an unknown Joint Action Committee to insult the person of the FCT Minister and accuse him of forging official documents of the government arising from a committee duly set up by his predecessor,” he said. He added that apart from the 2016 committee, another one was set up on December 17, 2020, following the university management’s visit to the FCT Minister on October 13, 2020. According to him, part of the recommendations of the December 2020 committee read: “Based on the recommended size of 100Ha for a University Campus stipulated by the National University Commission and considering that the University has held the title of about 11,608.33Ha for over thirty (30) years, a total of about 1,922.66Ha should be left to the University while the remaining part of the land should be designed and detailed by URP (Urban and Regional Planning) Department for compatible land use like Institution and Research Districts.” The recommendation went on: “This will solve the issues of continuous and unabated village expansion which will save the FCTA the unending trouble of village encroachments and the cost of removing them.” Olayinka said the issues the university presented to the 2016 committee included the issuance of Certificate of Occupancy for its main and mini campuses and its properties in Kado and Jahi districts. Others were Area Council layout within its campuses, indigenous and illegal settlements within the main campus land, and re-issuance of the title document of the mini campus, which got burnt during the 1994 students uprising. He said the December 2020 committee, which visited the university and other settlements within the over 11,000 hectares, “found that 805.7 hectares of the land had been occupied by villages while the Nigerian Army Welfare Limited Guarantee Housing Estate occupied 9.91 hectares.” “Also, about 500 hectares had already been approved for a main sewage treatment plant,” he said. On the Minister’s powers, Olayinka said: “In exercising his powers under the Land Use Act No. 6 of 1978, Capital. L5, Laws of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 2004, the FCT Minister does not even require any committee report. It is also not the duty of any workers union to be involved in the allocation of land to a university by the government, most importantly, a university owned by the government. “Government established a university, gave land to it and later saw the need to reduce the land to what it opined can be better managed and utilized by the university, workers unions with primary responsibility of welfare of its members are protesting. What exactly is their business? Were they consulted before the university was established and the land allocated in the first place? Of what effect is land occupied by university to its workers and students? “The university is owned by the government. The land is owned by the government. The meddlesome interlopers acting under this Joint Action Committee are workers and students employed or admitted by the university. When did it become the responsibility of an employee to fight an employer for choosing to reduce the land occupied by his own establishment? “Meanwhile, some of these union leaders have their children in private universities in Nigeria. How many of those private universities are built on more than 100 hectares of land?” he asked. While insisting that the protest was misplaced, he described as funny and strange a situation where university union leaders protest over land issues when other universities in the world are already operating virtually. “And if the land is so needed by the university, why did it allocate part of it to individuals and corporate organization, including the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission?” he queried. The post Unionism not a licence for irresponsibility, Wike’s aide slams UniAbuja staff appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: AI being run in a ‘mediaeval’ way – UN
item.description: Artificial intelligence is being governed in an almost mediaeval fashion, the UN rights chief warned Thursday, with power concentrated in the hands of a few tech barons. Speaking at the RightsX summit in Geneva, Volker Turk said that while the story of AI sounded futuristic, underneath it was an age-old narrative of power. “A handful of men still control much of the world’s AI computing power, data and infrastructure. And we still have no common rules to pace or steer AI development,” he said. Turk said there was a glaring democratic deficit when five technology companies owned more than 70 percent of global AI computing capacity. “We have the technology of the future governed in an almost mediaeval way: by a select few, with virtually no checks, no balances, no participation, and no accountability,” he said. “History has taught us: with this kind of power, the rights and freedoms of ordinary people are the first to suffer.” Reiterating his call for rights-centred AI regulation, the UN high commissioner for human rights said the technology was increasingly controlling people’s lives. And this, he warned, was often happening without their knowledge, and could distort public debate in “subtle, insidious ways”. Meanwhile biased algorithms could reproduce injustice on an industrial scale, he cautioned. – ‘Civilisational collapse’ – “Our transport, food and healthcare are increasingly digitised. We may not be far from the day when AI can cut off the critical infrastructure of entire communities or countries, either on its own or in the wrong hands,” Turk warned. “When people discuss the chances of civilisational collapse because of AI, we need to ask: who decides what chances we take?” He voiced optimism that people would ultimately challenge unchecked power, with the democratic deficit turning into a deficit of trust. He cited young people already stepping offline to regain greater control of their lives. Turk said AI’s benefits should be shared equitably, which would require goodwill from technology companies, but also regulation and accountability. He said he had written to frontier AI companies urging them to introduce effective safeguards “before it is too late”. Turk noted that a bottle of milk could not make it to a shop without layers of testing, rules and regulations. So for AI, “it’s a no-brainer that you need some form of regulation”, given its potential for harm, Turk said. As for how models are trained, he suggested giving the Universal Declaration of Human Rights “as the task to AI”. The post AI being run in a ‘mediaeval’ way – UN appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Gonzalo García: ‘I love Craven Cottage – the fans can reach out and touch you’
item.description: Spain Under-21 striker admits the pace of the Premier League has surprised him but says he must stay calm over goal drought at Fulham The first thing Rita Hayworth’s great nephew says when he walks in is: “Sorry I’m late.” Gonzalo García is not late, but it’s very like him: he is impeccably polite, accommodating, and there’s an almost gentle quality to him, a calm that’s not common but can help, especially in moments when the pressure builds. There’s a reason one of the coaches standing in the rain by the pitch where Spain’s under-21s have just finished training says everyone here loves García. The Fulham striker shakes hands, introduces himself and ducks into the dressing room to change; then a few minutes later he’s back, apologising for a wait that wasn’t one. Time to talk, so let’s start with tinseltown, the family tale. García laughs. His great-aunt, born Margarita Carmen Cansino, was among the biggest stars in Hollywood, although he’s not sure he’s seen any of her films. His grandfather was a surgeon and others in the family followed. His uncles played rugby for Spain, but that wasn’t his thing. As for him, he enrolled in a degree in business management and analytics, and reckons he might have liked law, yet even that wasn’t his chosen field. Continue reading...

item.title: 20 Years Ago, Nintendo’s Awkwardly Named Console Defied All Its Biggest Doubters
item.description: Nintendo is a force in the video game industry, currently riding high with the Switch 2 , but it has had dips and missteps like any other company. After strong performances during the 8-bit and 16-bit eras, its performance started to slip with the powerful Nintendo 64, which gave unexpected ground to the PlayStation console that Nintendo itself inspired Sony to build. Despite the GameCube’s impressive tech, the hardware continued to bleed market share to new competitors, and it was clear something needed to change to avoid a fate worse than Sega.

item.title: ‘No more playstation’ – Anthony Joshua welcomes baby girl
item.description: Nigerian-British boxing champion, Anthony Joshua, has announced the birth of his second child, a girl, noting that there is no more time for PlayStation or FIFA for him. Joshua and his childhood sweetheart, Nicole Osbourne, welcomed their daughter on November 14, 2026. The pair also have an 11-year-old son, Joseph. The former two-time unified heavyweight champion revealed this in an interview with The Sun , which gained attention on Thursday, said having a daughter would help him better understand women and how to support them. “Now I’ve got a daughter, I will get an insight and a bit more understanding of what it means to be a woman, and how I can be supportive. My daughter will give me firsthand experience of a woman’s power,” he said. Joshua disclosed that the family had yet to settle on a name for the newborn, but described her as his princess. “I’ve spoken to all the women in my family, and it’s amazing the amount of support that women give each other. We haven’t given her a name yet, but she’s my Princess,” he added. The 36 year old boxer described the birth as a huge blessing, revealing that he deliberately avoided finding out the baby’s sex during the pregnancy. “It’s been amazing, a big blessing and I can’t believe I’m a girl dad. I didn’t want to find the sex out during the pregnancy,” Joshua said. He also joked about how having a daughter could change some of the activities he shares with his son. “I love boys but as soon as I found out we had a little girl I said, ‘No more Fifa, no more motorbiking, no more PlayStation!’” he said. “I’m going to do it all, so you might see me with some eyeshadow on, some nail polish on, drinking some tea in a doll’s playhouse and just trying to do the right thing by her, you know?” he said. He also spoke about the responsibilities of caring for a newborn, saying he was prepared to change nappies and go through the demands of raising a baby again. “I will change nappies, I’ve gotta go through all that stinky bum time again!” he added. The development comes as Joshua prepares for a reported December 11 showdown with fellow British heavyweight boxer Tyson Fury. Vanguard News The post ‘No more playstation’ – Anthony Joshua welcomes baby girl appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Oil resumption: KAGOTE insists Ogoni people must ratify FG’s MoU
item.description: …Group welcomes Tinubu’s intervention on Eleme section of East-West Road By Daniel Abia, Port Harcourt The leadership of KAGOTE, comprising Khana, Gokana, Tai and Eleme local government areas of Rivers State, has insisted that the proposed Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between the Federal Government and the Ogoni people on the resumption of oil exploration in Ogoniland must be ratified by the people before it is signed. The group said the contents of the proposed agreement must be presented to the Ogoni people for approval to secure their mandate and ensure the legitimacy of the process. KAGOTE President, Chief Lesi Ma-ol, stated this in a statement, explaining that it had been agreed that congresses should be convened in Khana, Gokana, Tai and Eleme by their duly elected local government chairmen to consider and ratify the proposed agreement. He said the arrangement would address concerns over the legality and legitimacy of the Ogoni Dialogue Committee (ODC) and provide a platform for the people to approve the MoU with the Federal Government. Ma-ol stressed the need for unity within the ODC, insisting that no individual or group of members should sign any agreement on behalf of the committee without its collective approval and ratification by the congresses. “We consider the unity of the ODC as essential, as such it was resolved that we shall sign as a collective. No member or group of members shall, by themselves, sign any document on behalf of the ODC that has not been adopted by the ODC and approved/ratified by the congresses. “We are totally in support of the resumption of oil and gas exploration in Ogoniland. We are committed to ensuring that the necessary foundations are properly laid. We want a resumption that brings peace, security, employment, economic opportunities, environmental responsibility and sustainable development to our land,” he said. The KAGOTE president said President Bola Tinubu initiated the peace process with good intentions, adding that the group was committed to doing everything possible to ensure its success. He, however, said a sustainable outcome must be built on trust, inclusiveness, transparency and the legitimate mandate of the Ogoni people. Ma-ol explained that KAGOTE was currently involved in harmonising the Federal Government’s response to the demands of the Ogoni people, a process expected to culminate in the proposed MoU. item.content:encoded: …Group welcomes Tinubu’s intervention on Eleme section of East-West Road By Daniel Abia, Port Harcourt The leadership of KAGOTE, comprising Khana, Gokana, Tai and Eleme local government areas of Rivers State, has insisted that the proposed Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between the Federal Government and the Ogoni people on the resumption of oil exploration in Ogoniland must be ratified by the people before it is signed. The group said the contents of the proposed agreement must be presented to the Ogoni people for approval to secure their mandate and ensure the legitimacy of the process. KAGOTE President, Chief Lesi Ma-ol, stated this in a statement, explaining that it had been agreed that congresses should be convened in Khana, Gokana, Tai and Eleme by their duly elected local government chairmen to consider and ratify the proposed agreement. He said the arrangement would address concerns over the legality and legitimacy of the Ogoni Dialogue Committee (ODC) and provide a platform for the people to approve the MoU with the Federal Government. Ma-ol stressed the need for unity within the ODC, insisting that no individual or group of members should sign any agreement on behalf of the committee without its collective approval and ratification by the congresses. “We consider the unity of the ODC as essential, as such it was resolved that we shall sign as a collective. No member or group of members shall, by themselves, sign any document on behalf of the ODC that has not been adopted by the ODC and approved/ratified by the congresses. “We are totally in support of the resumption of oil and gas exploration in Ogoniland. We are committed to ensuring that the necessary foundations are properly laid. We want a resumption that brings peace, security, employment, economic opportunities, environmental responsibility and sustainable development to our land,” he said. The KAGOTE president said President Bola Tinubu initiated the peace process with good intentions, adding that the group was committed to doing everything possible to ensure its success. He, however, said a sustainable outcome must be built on trust, inclusiveness, transparency and the legitimate mandate of the Ogoni people. Ma-ol explained that KAGOTE was currently involved in harmonising the Federal Government’s response to the demands of the Ogoni people, a process expected to culminate in the proposed MoU. He said the group had consistently advocated the implementation of confidence-building measures agreed upon with the Federal Government, including employment opportunities, schools, hospital renovations and other development projects, alongside the Eleme section of the East-West Road. According to him, several of the projects remain stalled, with their levels of completion ranging from zero to about 40 per cent. He, however, expressed delight that the group’s persistent advocacy had begun to yield results, particularly following the release of funds by Tinubu for the continuation of work on the Eleme section of the East-West Road. “We are particularly pleased that on Friday, 13th November 2026, Mr President released funds for the continuation of work on the Eleme section of the East-West Road. “We deeply appreciate this intervention and regard it as an encouraging development. We pray that the release will translate into sustained work until the road is completed and that the other confidence-building commitments will equally receive the necessary attention,” he said. Ma-ol said the intervention reinforced the group’s belief that its advocacy for the fulfilment of the Federal Government’s commitments was on the right track. He added that the implementation of the confidence-building measures was necessary to establish the trust and goodwill required for a peaceful and sustainable resumption of oil and gas activities in Ogoniland. On the proposed MoU, the KAGOTE president said a review of the draft submitted by the Federal Government had revealed certain provisions requiring clarification because of their implications for the agreement and its implementation. “We believe therefore that these must be properly addressed to ensure that the document reflects the understandings reached and adequately protects the corporate interests and legitimate aspirations of the Ogoni people,” he said. item.title: Cyberattack on service provider exposes payee data at 40 Irish credit unions
item.description: An attack on software provider Wellington IT exposed saved payee details held by around 40 Irish credit unions, prompting a minister to criticize the company's delay in notifying them. Robert Troy, Ireland's minister of state with responsibility for credit unions, said the breach happened in October but many affected institutions only learned of it in recent days. Troy told Irish broadcaster RTÉ that the breach occurred "sometime in October," and Wellington IT's delay in providing details to its credit union customers was "not acceptable." News of the issues affecting Irish credit unions broke on Tuesday, although the government said at the time it was only investigating a "possible cybersecurity incident" in the first instance, and did not name Wellington IT until Wednesday. Affected credit unions said attackers exploited a vulnerability in their provider's online banking platform between October 2 and 4. The flaw was closed on October 6. Troy said the affected credit unions were only informed for the first time in recent days. The exposed records concern payees saved in members' online banking accounts. Those records can also be linked to the members who created them. The information exposed varies between institutions and individual records, but disclosures list the following data types: Names on payee bank accounts and saved nicknames Business Identifier Codes (BICs) International Bank Account Numbers (IBANs) Sort codes Payment references Internal reference numbers that do not identify customers Payee addresses Credit unions including St. Canice's said online banking passwords, PINs, and login credentials were unaffected, and that the exposed payee details did not provide access to members' accounts or funds. St. Canice's warned members not to transfer money in response to anyone claiming it needed to be moved to safety because of the breach. The CEO of Belfast-based Wellington IT, Colin Mitchell, said in a statement that the company notified the affected organizations "as soon as we confirmed the potential risk to customer data." He said Wellington IT has engaged outside cybersecurity experts to help investigate the breach, and reported the matter to the relevant authorities. Mitchell added: "We are directly supporting our customers in their assessment of the potential impact on affected individuals and to help them meet any applicable regulatory obligations. "We recognize the importance of this matter to our customers and their members and are treating it with the utmost seriousness. We remain focused on completing a thorough investigation and communicating directly with our customers as the investigation progresses." Owned by Canadian company Vencora, Wellington IT has offices in Belfast and Dublin, and provides credit unions with software, mobile apps, private cloud infrastructure, and fully managed services. Around 40 credit unions in Ireland were affected, roughly a quarter of the national total, Troy said. Credit unions operate similar

Robert Troy, Ireland's minister of state with responsibility for credit unions, said the breach happened in October but many affected institutions only learned of it in recent days. Troy told Irish broadcaster RTÉ that the breach occurred "sometime in October," and Wellington IT's delay in providing details to its credit union customers was "not acceptable." News of the issues affecting Irish credit unions broke on Tuesday, although the government said at the time it was only investigating a "possible cybersecurity incident" in the first instance, and did not name Wellington IT until Wednesday. Affected credit unions said attackers exploited a vulnerability in their provider's online banking platform between October 2 and 4. The flaw was closed on October 6. Troy said the affected credit unions were only informed for the first time in recent days. The exposed records concern payees saved in members' online banking accounts. Those records can also be linked to the members who created them. The information exposed varies between institutions and individual records, but disclosures list the following data types: Names on payee bank accounts and saved nicknames Business Identifier Codes (BICs) International Bank Account Numbers (IBANs) Sort codes Payment references Internal reference numbers that do not identify customers Payee addresses Credit unions including St. Canice's said online banking passwords, PINs, and login credentials were unaffected, and that the exposed payee details did not provide access to members' accounts or funds. St. Canice's warned members not to transfer money in response to anyone claiming it needed to be moved to safety because of the breach. The CEO of Belfast-based Wellington IT, Colin Mitchell, said in a statement that the company notified the affected organizations "as soon as we confirmed the potential risk to customer data." He said Wellington IT has engaged outside cybersecurity experts to help investigate the breach, and reported the matter to the relevant authorities. Mitchell added: "We are directly supporting our customers in their assessment of the potential impact on affected individuals and to help them meet any applicable regulatory obligations. "We recognize the importance of this matter to our customers and their members and are treating it with the utmost seriousness. We remain focused on completing a thorough investigation and communicating directly with our customers as the investigation progresses." Owned by Canadian company Vencora, Wellington IT has offices in Belfast and Dublin, and provides credit unions with software, mobile apps, private cloud infrastructure, and fully managed services. Around 40 credit unions in Ireland were affected, roughly a quarter of the national total, Troy said. Credit unions operate similarly to traditional banks, offering savings accounts and loans, but are owned by their members and are not-for-profit organizations. Troy told RTÉ that cybersecurity is a constant challenge for financial institutions, as technology and threats evolve over time. "What's most important is that financial institutions take all the right measures to mitigate against these threats and that is what is happening," he said. Separately, the UK's Financial Conduct Authority, Prudential Regulation Authority, and Bank of England opened a joint consultation on cyber resilience guidance on Thursday. The FCA said October brought its second-highest monthly tally of reported cyber incidents in five years, and the highest in 18 months. The proposed guidance clarifies how firms should meet existing requirements rather than introducing new rules. ®

item.title: Mera denies defection rumour to APC in Kebbi
item.description: By Haruna Aliyu, Birnin Kebbi The African Democratic Congress (ADC) senatorial candidate for Kebbi North, Alhaji Ibrahim Muhammad Mera, has dismissed reports circulating on social media that he has defected to the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) in Kebbi State. Mera, in a statement signed by his Director-General, Media, Garba Muhammad Yeldu, on Thursday, said he had neither met nor held discussions with any APC official or member over a possible defection. He described the reports as fabricated, alleging that they were being circulated by individuals seeking to create confusion and distract him from pursuing his senatorial ambition under the ADC. Mera acknowledged that political parties were experiencing internal challenges but insisted that the crisis within the ADC would not make him abandon the party. He said the APC also had its internal disagreements, adding that he remained focused on his political ambition and the pursuit of the Kebbi North senatorial seat. The ADC candidate urged his supporters and constituents to disregard the reports, describing them as products of the rumour peddlers’ imagination. He also appealed to them to remain calm, peaceful and law-abiding while continuing to support the ADC. “I have never for once thought or made attempts to leave ADC. I remain focused and unrelenting in the pursuit of my mandate in my party,” he said. Mera warned those behind the reports to desist from spreading what he described as false information and assured his supporters of his continued loyalty to the ADC. The post Mera denies defection rumour to APC in Kebbi appeared first on Vanguard News .

The ADC candidate urged his supporters and constituents to disregard the reports, describing them as products of the rumour peddlers’ imagination. He also appealed to them to remain calm, peaceful and law-abiding while continuing to support the ADC. “I have never for once thought or made attempts to leave ADC. I remain focused and unrelenting in the pursuit of my mandate in my party,” he said. Mera warned those behind the reports to desist from spreading what he described as false information and assured his supporters of his continued loyalty to the ADC. item.title: How to tell a cyberattack from a plain old outage
item.description: Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a Diehard IV –style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US. Across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies , a Federal Aviation Administration tech screw-up grounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified network’s downtime left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade. In the midst of a US war with Iran and rising fears of AI-enabled hacking , this still-unfolding comedy of IT errors colliding across American infrastructure felt to plenty of observers like more than a coincidence. Yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack. Read full article Comments

item.title: What's next for NASA interstellar Voyager 1 probe after passing 1 light-day from Earth?
item.description: null Voyager 1 has reached a historic milestone in space — it now takes a light-day to send a command to the spacecraft, meaning a full 24 hours for Earth to hail the distant spacecraft. Since Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2 , launched on an initial tour through the outer solar system in 1977, their missions have been packed with science. Voyager 1 looked at Jupiter and Saturn from up close before veering for a flyby of Saturn's moon Titan and Saturn's rings, a pathway that brought it above the plane of the solar system in the early 1980s. Voyager 1's faster path out of the solar system brought it to one light-day in distance on Wednesday (Nov. 18), while Voyager 2 — which took a slightly slower track to see Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — will reach a light-day of distance in 2035. So what's next for the two Voyager spacecraft as they reach further into interstellar space? Exploring afar Interstellar space, which is the area where the sun's constant stream of solar particles within the heliopause gives way to the physics of interstellar space, has been a valuable harvest for both Voyagers. Voyager 1 crossed interstellar space in August 2012 and continues to get data, while Voyager 2 has done the same since November 2018. "Current science is continuing our investigation on magnetic field strength and direction, plasma density, and energetic particle detection. What is important is to measure how these phenomena change as the spacecraft travels further away from the sun," Suzanne Dodd, project manager for the Voyager missions at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), told Space.com in an email. Added to that will be the Voyagers' examinations of plasma and magnetic fields nearby the spacecraft, and a focus on any "solar effects" such as shocks or pressure fronts, added JPL project scientist Linda Spilker in an email. "Key Voyager science going forward includes observing the extent to which our sun continues to affect interstellar space, all the way out to Voyager 1," Spilker continued. "Where does the sun's influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may last long enough to answer that question." The team also wants to watch the magnetic field around the spacecraft continue to change direction from the sun, to interstellar space, Spilker noted. That finding was not expected when the Voyagers launched, so scientists are curious to know more — as long as the spacecraft can last, that is. The locations of Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 beyond the boundary of our solar system. (Image credit: NASA, ESA, and Z. item.dc:creator: Elizabeth Howell
item.content:encoded: null Voyager 1 has reached a historic milestone in space — it now takes a light-day to send a command to the spacecraft, meaning a full 24 hours for Earth to hail the distant spacecraft. Since Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2 , launched on an initial tour through the outer solar system in 1977, their missions have been packed with science. Voyager 1 looked at Jupiter and Saturn from up close before veering for a flyby of Saturn's moon Titan and Saturn's rings, a pathway that brought it above the plane of the solar system in the early 1980s. Voyager 1's faster path out of the solar system brought it to one light-day in distance on Wednesday (Nov. 18), while Voyager 2 — which took a slightly slower track to see Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — will reach a light-day of distance in 2035. So what's next for the two Voyager spacecraft as they reach further into interstellar space? Exploring afar Interstellar space, which is the area where the sun's constant stream of solar particles within the heliopause gives way to the physics of interstellar space, has been a valuable harvest for both Voyagers. Voyager 1 crossed interstellar space in August 2012 and continues to get data, while Voyager 2 has done the same since November 2018. "Current science is continuing our investigation on magnetic field strength and direction, plasma density, and energetic particle detection. What is important is to measure how these phenomena change as the spacecraft travels further away from the sun," Suzanne Dodd, project manager for the Voyager missions at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), told Space.com in an email. Added to that will be the Voyagers' examinations of plasma and magnetic fields nearby the spacecraft, and a focus on any "solar effects" such as shocks or pressure fronts, added JPL project scientist Linda Spilker in an email. "Key Voyager science going forward includes observing the extent to which our sun continues to affect interstellar space, all the way out to Voyager 1," Spilker continued. "Where does the sun's influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may last long enough to answer that question." The team also wants to watch the magnetic field around the spacecraft continue to change direction from the sun, to interstellar space, Spilker noted. That finding was not expected when the Voyagers launched, so scientists are curious to know more — as long as the spacecraft can last, that is. The locations of Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 beyond the boundary of our solar system. (Image credit: NASA, ESA, and Z. Levay (STScI)) Power management Each Voyager continues to lose 4 watts of power a year; their launch power was 470 watts in 1977, and the nuclear power source continues to dwindle, requiring harder choices as the missions approach their 50th years of operations. Instruments have had to be shut off, and both the spacecraft were directed to perform a "Big Bang" of power redistribution earlier this year to preserve as much power as possible without sacrificing science. Looking forward, Dodd says the team does not anticipate having to make any major changes to spacecraft operations until after the 50th anniversary passes for each spacecraft next August and September (as Voyager 2 launched a few weeks before Voyager 1). An image of Saturn captured by Voyager on Nov. 16, 1980 four days after the probe's closest approach to the planet, taken from a distance of 3,300,000 miles (5,300,000 kilometers). (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) A JPL representative added that the "Big Bang" should keep the remaining science instruments going until that point, although "there is also the thermal state of the spacecraft to balance." The representative added that the margins for power remain "very thin," especially as the spacecraft are quite cold in interstellar space. "Then there are the things the team can't predict, such as the unexpected loss of contact that happened recently," the spokesperson added, referring to an approximately 48-hour glitch in which Voyager 1 suddenly stopped responding to commands last month — although the spacecraft did quickly recover. "The goal of the mission is science, so the team is not just concerned with keeping in contact with the Voyagers, but keeping the science instruments going as long as possible," the representative added. "The further away the spacecraft get from Earth, the more they learn about how interstellar space changes further away from the heliopause." Voyager 2 in a clean room being worked on by engineers on March 23, 1977. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) The legacy of Voyager 1 Voyager 1 team members now represent multiple generations of engineers, each one of them with distinct but essential roles. Even the most junior members of the team—Nshan Kazaryan and Bhavana Gupta—are taking on key roles in anticipation of more responsibility in the future, according to JPL mission manager Kareem Badaruddin. "They have demonstrated their value to the team consistently," Badaruddin said in an email. Kazaryan's responsibilities include negotiating tracking schedules with the Deep Space Network (DSN), a set of three antennas for following distant missions, to keep tabs on the Voyagers. Gupta, meanwhile, has provided documentation to gather important details from the Voyagers' command and control systems to "give detailed instructions" in case of issues. "One of our most senior team members, Jack Lippincott, has provided critical knowledge and understanding of DSN operations and data interpretation," Badaruddin added. Pointing to one of the DSN antennas in Goldstone, Australia, he said the weather in that region "has been violent the last few weeks, and he has helped us to understand how to deal with unique problems that arose because of it." While there's no real sense of how much further the spacecraft could keep going, the team says it's committed to be there as long as possible. "It has taken decades of exceptional engineering to get Voyager 1 to the one light-day milestone, and hopefully much further before the mission ends," Dodd said. Badaruddin added: "One of the reasons that one light-day is so special is that it has never happened before that we were in contact with a spacecraft at this distance, and it may never happen again."

item.title: TfL takes Oyster photocard website offline after attackers compromise customer accounts
item.description: Transport for London (TfL) has copped to another cybersecurity breach, this time involving the account details of around 265,000 Oyster photocard customers. The capital's transport operator told The Register it first became aware something was amiss on November 16, when Oyster photocard customers started receiving emails asking them to create accounts they already had. The emails came from TfL's own systems, the transport body confirmed, but were generated as a result of the compromise. "We immediately took the TfL photocard website down while this was being investigated," said Shashi Verma, TfL's director of technology strategy and revenue. "The protection of personal information is a priority for us, and I apologize to our customers affected by this incident." TfL reckons its speedy response spared a considerable number of customers from having their details compromised. The transport operator says it has since contained the incident and contacted those potentially affected, though it is rather more forthcoming about what the hackers didn't get their hands on than what they did. TfL says no passwords, bank or payment card details, or customer journey information were compromised. It also believes the names and dates of birth of children with Zip Oyster cards were unaffected. Among those whose accounts may have been compromised are holders of Zip Oyster cards – issued to children as young as five – as well as students, apprentices, care leavers, veterans, and Londoners aged 60 and over. Despite the assurances about passwords, TfL says it will ask all photocard customers to change theirs, along with their security questions and answers. Those in the habit of recycling passwords across multiple websites are being advised to change them elsewhere, too. TfL says it has yet to find any evidence that the compromised data has been used and has notified the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO). The transport operator hasn't disclosed how the perpetrators got into its systems. Existing photocards will still let holders through the ticket barriers, though anyone needing to renew one or check their journey history will have to contact TfL's customer services team while the website is out of action . There's no word yet on when it'll be back. "We hope to restore the affected website services as quickly as possible," Verma said. TfL should be well versed in dealing with data breaches by now. In March, the transport operator told The Register it had notified more than 7 million customers following its September 2024 cyberattack. The hackers had accessed systems holding customers' names, email addresses, and home addresses, while around 5,000 customers were contacted as a priority because their bank account details may also have been compromised. Two teenagers were subsequently charged in connection with the attack, which authorities linked to the notorious Scattered Spider cybercrime crew. The ICO looked into that incident but opted not to take enforcement

item.title: Inside women’s football’s difficult rise in Syria: ‘A joy that everyone in the country needed’
item.description: A 14-year civil war ravaged the country and ground women’s football to a halt. Today, the first glimmers of hope are beginning to emerge amid difficulty In December 2024, Syria’s under-18 women’s football team boarded a last-minute bus at midnight from Aqaba, bound for Damascus. The players had been in Jordan preparing for their final match of the WAFF women’s championship, where a win against Saudi Arabia would have kept their hopes of winning the title alive. Syria pulled out amid fears that the border would close. Back home, a war that had been largely frozen for four years was suddenly moving at pace. Rebel forces had swept out of the northwest, taking Aleppo and were pushing south towards the capital, 350km away, threatening to topple the now-former president, Bashar al-Assad. Players from the provinces around Damascus made their way home. But those from Hasakah, in the country’s far north-east, spent the next three days stranded at Damascus airport, as airline staff fled and planes sat idle on the tarmac, until a bus was finally able to take them home. Continue reading...

item.title: Esther Adeyanju: This International Men’s Day, Let’s Make Room for Men’s Vulnerability
item.description: “Men are not wired to show emotions.” A male friend once said to me during an argument. He was so convinced that I wondered whether a manual somewhere explained how men were manufactured. According to him, men were created to be strong, endure pain and keep their emotions to themselves. That was simply how they were made. “So, because you’re a man, you’re not supposed to feel hurt, fear or disappointment?” I disagreed. He insisted that showing emotions was not in a man’s nature. Who made that rule? Who decided that men could experience pain but must never be seen expressing it? At what point did being a man become synonymous with pretending that everything was fine? The conversation wilted, but it has stayed with me, perhaps because my friend wasn’t expressing an unusual opinion. He was repeating a stereotype many of us have heard all our lives: “Boys don’t cry.” “Be a man.” “Man up.” Three little expressions, and somewhere between being told to be strong and learning to say “I’m fine,” I wonder how many men have forgotten what it feels like to be heard. Frequent questions men are asked: “How far? Work nko?” “When are you getting married?” “Have you bought land?” “How is the family?” And the famous Nigerian question that can make an unemployed graduate dread family gatherings: “So, what are you doing now?” We often inquire about their achievements, responsibilities, and plans. These aspects are important, but how often do we ask about their fears? A father who leaves home before sunrise and returns exhausted, burdened by the weight of school fees, rent, and family expectations. A young graduate who has submitted countless job applications, yet still smiles politely when another relative inquires why he hasn’t found a job. A successful professional whose LinkedIn profile showcases numerous achievements, while his personal life tells a story that no one has thought to ask about. We admire their strength, we applaud their sacrifices, and we celebrate their accomplishments. But what about what they are going through? The person everyone leans on also needs somewhere to lean. Society has an interesting checklist for measuring a man’s success. A good job, a house, a car, a wife, children and financial stability. Preferably, all achieved before a certain age. But if a man struggles to achieve all these, is his life any less meaningful? Surely, a man’s worth cannot be reduced to his bank balance, job title or ability to convince everyone that he has everything under control. There must be room for men who are still becoming. item.dc:creator: BellaNaija Features
item.content:encoded: “Men are not wired to show emotions.” A male friend once said to me during an argument. He was so convinced that I wondered whether a manual somewhere explained how men were manufactured. According to him, men were created to be strong, endure pain and keep their emotions to themselves. That was simply how they were made. “So, because you’re a man, you’re not supposed to feel hurt, fear or disappointment?” I disagreed. He insisted that showing emotions was not in a man’s nature. Who made that rule? Who decided that men could experience pain but must never be seen expressing it? At what point did being a man become synonymous with pretending that everything was fine? The conversation wilted, but it has stayed with me, perhaps because my friend wasn’t expressing an unusual opinion. He was repeating a stereotype many of us have heard all our lives: “Boys don’t cry.” “Be a man.” “Man up.” Three little expressions, and somewhere between being told to be strong and learning to say “I’m fine,” I wonder how many men have forgotten what it feels like to be heard. Frequent questions men are asked: “How far? Work nko?” “When are you getting married?” “Have you bought land?” “How is the family?” And the famous Nigerian question that can make an unemployed graduate dread family gatherings: “So, what are you doing now?” We often inquire about their achievements, responsibilities, and plans. These aspects are important, but how often do we ask about their fears? A father who leaves home before sunrise and returns exhausted, burdened by the weight of school fees, rent, and family expectations. A young graduate who has submitted countless job applications, yet still smiles politely when another relative inquires why he hasn’t found a job. A successful professional whose LinkedIn profile showcases numerous achievements, while his personal life tells a story that no one has thought to ask about. We admire their strength, we applaud their sacrifices, and we celebrate their accomplishments. But what about what they are going through? The person everyone leans on also needs somewhere to lean. Society has an interesting checklist for measuring a man’s success. A good job, a house, a car, a wife, children and financial stability. Preferably, all achieved before a certain age. But if a man struggles to achieve all these, is his life any less meaningful? Surely, a man’s worth cannot be reduced to his bank balance, job title or ability to convince everyone that he has everything under control. There must be room for men who are still becoming. The Empty Chair Nobody Notices This year’s theme for International Men’s Day, celebrated on November 19th, is “The Future Is Everyone.” While this theme may seem straightforward, it invites us to explore the true meaning of “everyone.” Working in corporate communications at the Chartered Institute of Personnel Management of Nigeria (CIPM) has heightened my awareness of how easily we categorise people based on their roles: leaders, employees, fathers, mothers, young professionals, and others. However, behind every label is a human being whose story is often more complex than it appears. The theme urges us to see people beyond face value, beyond titles and see them as humans first. It urges us to avoid assuming we know what others need. Allowing men to share their struggles does not diminish the experiences of another gender. Compassion is not a competition; there is ample space to challenge the expectations that confine both men and women. After all, what kind of future can belong to everyone if some individuals must conceal parts of themselves to fit in? This International Men’s Day, let’s celebrate the men who show up for their families, mentor young people, support their communities, and quietly make life better for others. Let’s remember the weary men—those who haven’t achieved everything they envisioned, who fear disappointing their families, and who desperately need help but have been taught that asking for assistance makes them less of a man. Reach out to your brother, check in on your father, and connect with that friend who always seems to have everything figured out. I still disagree with my friend’s belief that men were not created to show emotions. Men are human beings, not machines programmed to absorb every disappointment without showing vulnerability. If the future truly belongs to everyone, it must also include men who are allowed to be vulnerable, uncertain, imperfect, and human. We have spent generations teaching men to stand strong, but it’s time we remind them that they don’t always have to stand alone. item.title: APEC Summit: Lots of gloss, little real progress?
item.description: Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin are holding their first-ever trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the APEC forum. It is a historic moment in more ways than one, with the leaders of the world’s three most powerful countries around the same table. Ukraine, the war in Iran, nuclear disarmament and artificial intelligence are all expected to be discussed, and the summit has stoked fears of a carve-up of the world into spheres of influence. But despite the buzz, analysts expect more symbolism than substance, with few concrete breakthroughs likely. Our correspondent in the region has more.

item.title: Xi, Trump, Putin: historic summit ends, outcome unclear
item.description: The unprecedented trilateral summit between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin ended on Thursday in Shenzhen after about an hour and 20 minutes. No details have emerged yet, but the three leaders talking face to face is already an event. Each has their own agenda: Putin wants to be back on the world stage, Trump needs a win at home, and Xi is asserting China’s status as an economic superpower. What comes out of it remains unclear, as FRANCE 24's journalists explain.

item.description: In an interview with FRANCE 24, former FIFA president Joseph (Sepp) Blatter claimed that Gianni Infantino "is not eligible" to run in the upcoming election for FIFA president because he's running for the fourth time, which is forbidden "according to the existing statutes of FIFA". Blatter also accused Infantino of buying votes and of "using FIFA's money to go from one country to the other to decide them to sign for him".

item.title: Sticky note on monitor provided keys to the company’s kingdom
item.description: Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where we talk smack about organizations that have smacked themselves down by practicing poor security hygiene. This week's story involves everyone's favorite low-tech password manager: the sticky note. Our terrifying tale comes courtesy of Christian Espinosa, a certified penetration tester with over 30 years of experience and the CEO of Blue Goat Cyber , a security company. Espinosa shared an experience where critical credentials were right out in the open for any person in the office to see. During a walkthrough of a client's office, he noticed a password written on a sticky note that was taped to an employee's monitor. While writing down your password and placing it in a physically secure paper notebook might be ok, taping it to the computer is definitely not. "Before I get my fingers on any system, I first walk the physical area that the system is located in — attackers do that when they're looking at a target too," Espinosa explained. “Physical security vulnerabilities are neglected much more often than technical security vulnerabilities and firms invest in firewalls where a sticky note is placed 3 feet from the front door." Espinosa took a photo of the sticky note and immediately tried logging into that employee's account. Success. Then, he tried the very same password on the VPN, which apparently had been maintained by that employee. Once he connected to the VPN, Espinosa had full access to the company network and all of its shared drives. He opened a shared drive that this employee had access to and there was an HR folder with all kinds of personally identifiable information (PII) about employees, including home addresses, driver's licenses, and scanned W-4 forms. There were even spreadsheets that listed everyone's salaries. The employee account also had access to a document that contained a list of internal server names and the names of the people in charge of each server (great for phishing). Another document had instructions for how to log into the accounting server specifically. The accounting server was a particular treasure trove of client information. On that server, Espinosa found a folder with vendor banking information, invoices, and payment records. "At that point, a password I had read from a sticky note during a walk-through had taken me from one desk to information that could have been used for payroll fraud, identity theft, or vendor-payment fraud," Espinosa said. After getting access to all this information, the pen tester presented his findings to the client. They quickly disabled the rogue account and started reviewing VPN access logs to see who else might have gotten into the network. They then searched the office to see if anyone else was exposing a password on a sticky note. Finally, they tightened permissions on the HR and accounting shares so that only people who really needed access to that data could get in. The lessons here are pretty obvious. item.content:encoded: Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where we talk smack about organizations that have smacked themselves down by practicing poor security hygiene. This week's story involves everyone's favorite low-tech password manager: the sticky note. Our terrifying tale comes courtesy of Christian Espinosa, a certified penetration tester with over 30 years of experience and the CEO of Blue Goat Cyber , a security company. Espinosa shared an experience where critical credentials were right out in the open for any person in the office to see. During a walkthrough of a client's office, he noticed a password written on a sticky note that was taped to an employee's monitor. While writing down your password and placing it in a physically secure paper notebook might be ok, taping it to the computer is definitely not. "Before I get my fingers on any system, I first walk the physical area that the system is located in — attackers do that when they're looking at a target too," Espinosa explained. “Physical security vulnerabilities are neglected much more often than technical security vulnerabilities and firms invest in firewalls where a sticky note is placed 3 feet from the front door." Espinosa took a photo of the sticky note and immediately tried logging into that employee's account. Success. Then, he tried the very same password on the VPN, which apparently had been maintained by that employee. Once he connected to the VPN, Espinosa had full access to the company network and all of its shared drives. He opened a shared drive that this employee had access to and there was an HR folder with all kinds of personally identifiable information (PII) about employees, including home addresses, driver's licenses, and scanned W-4 forms. There were even spreadsheets that listed everyone's salaries. The employee account also had access to a document that contained a list of internal server names and the names of the people in charge of each server (great for phishing). Another document had instructions for how to log into the accounting server specifically. The accounting server was a particular treasure trove of client information. On that server, Espinosa found a folder with vendor banking information, invoices, and payment records. "At that point, a password I had read from a sticky note during a walk-through had taken me from one desk to information that could have been used for payroll fraud, identity theft, or vendor-payment fraud," Espinosa said. After getting access to all this information, the pen tester presented his findings to the client. They quickly disabled the rogue account and started reviewing VPN access logs to see who else might have gotten into the network. They then searched the office to see if anyone else was exposing a password on a sticky note. Finally, they tightened permissions on the HR and accounting shares so that only people who really needed access to that data could get in. The lessons here are pretty obvious. Don't expose your passwords and, perhaps even more importantly, limit who has access to file shares that contain mission-critical data such as employee or client information. "The part that really got the client's attention was how easily the attack could have continued after I left the building," Espinosa posited. "Someone could have photographed that sticky note, walked out, connected to the VPN later that night, and started going through employee and financial records from somewhere else." ®
