item.content:encoded: It’s Thanksgiving time, and we’re giving thanks to you for doing NASA Science with us! You and NASA’s other volunteers have enabled an incredible banquet of discoveries—by taking data, analyzing data, writing code, writing papers, and even inventing your own science projects. Whether you’re an expert participant or someone who’s just started your science journey, we’re deeply grateful for your help. Here are a few more messages of gratitude our scientists sent in to share with you. Chihoko Cullens, principal investigator (PI) of the Space Cloud Watch project, said: “Thank you to Pirjo Koski, Huub Eggen, and Brian Scott ! Pirjo posts beautiful Noctilucent Cloud photos and has introduced us to other cloud databases in the Netherlands. Huub goes beyond basic data requested by us and actively discusses his observations providing helpful insights. Brian contributes consistently and has provided us with useful time-lapse videos. All three volunteers have consistently provided much needed data and have contributed their time in developing our Field Guide that now helps new citizen scientists correctly identify and report their observations. We are grateful for their contributions.” Ryan Scott from the Open Science Data Repository Analysis Working Groups (OSDR AWGs) project said: “A cohort of high school students took NASA’s free Machine Learning for Space Biology course and then kept working as citizen science volunteers. Guided by OSDR AWG members​ who also gave their time freely, they mined open-access retinal data from the International Space Station (ISS) Rodent Research-9 Mission in the NASA Open Science Data Repository and trained a machine learning ensemble that separates oxidative damage from cell death in the eyes of space-flown mice, now published in the scientific journal npj Microgravity : Machine learning ensemble reveals distinct molecular pathways of retinal damage in spaceflown mice . Every citizen science student co-author earned authorship, and many of those listed above started college this fall with a NASA publication already behind them. Thanks to Aditi Adapala, Mushtaq Ali, Naomi Z. Chang, Sophie Cai, Margaret Hitt, Anishka Jain, Matthew Lin, MarcAnthony Paolieri Della Monica, Elior Paley, Rudransh Pathak, Shawnak Samaddar, Shriya Sawant, Zhihan Shi, Rohin Sood, Fabian P. Uribe, Maxwell Volkan, and Jessica Wu, plus OSDR AWG members Anna Lewkowicz, Sunny Narayanan, Daniya Thomas, Ethan Waisberg, Pinar Avci, Joshua Ong, Marshall Tabetah, Richard Barker, Lauren Sanders, and Xiao Wen ‘Vivien’ Mao.” Kyra Shaw, project coordinator for Snapshot Wisconsin at the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources, said: “Our team has a Thanksgiving thank-you message for Snapshot volunteer Tim Sparks. Tim has been a dedicated Snapshot Wisconsin volunteer for nearly 10 years. Tim went above and beyond these past two years by helping to pilot test protocols and then joining the full launch for a new initiative, the Snapshot Phenology Project. Joining a select group of volunteers, Tim set up and is maintaining extra equipment to measure snow depth, temperature, and sound recordings at his Snapshot trail camera site. Thank you, Tim, for joining in our events, sending in your favorite photos, and going the extra mile to make the Snapshot Phenology Project a success!” Benjamin Fernando from the Impact Flash! project said: “Thank you to everyone who’s been sending in images of the Moon! A special thanks to Joerg Tomczak, who helped us with the Artemis II campaign!” Rachael Mady from the Chesapeake Water Watch project said: “We are so thankful for all of our volunteers! Since 2021, volunteers have been with us every step of the way and have made Chesapeake Water Watch possible. The Chesapeake Bay is the nation’s largest estuary, and we had people all over submitting observations and helping us cross our 6,000 observation milestone this year. While the project may be wrapping up, the impact that our volunteers have on improving the health of the Bay will continue for years to come. Thanks for all that you do!” Marc Kuchner, from the Backyard Worlds: Planet 9 science team, said: “Thank you to Prateek Singh for creating new tools for astronomy and for helping us lead our Space Apps challenge! Thank you to Bruce Baller and Katharina Doll for sharing their lists of brown dwarf discoveries and for inspiring all of us! Thank you to Frank Kiwy for his latest batch of python tools – shared with everyone – that dig through Pan-STARRS, WISE, SIMBAD, Gaia DR3, CatWISE, and NSC DR2 data! Thank you to Michiharu Hyogo for keeping the new publications coming, Hugo Durantini Luca, Jim Rabe, and Lisa Stiller for helping keep us all connected, Peter Jalowiczor for traveling around the world in the snow, and to Farid Cedeno and Martin Bilsing for teaching others about our project!” Emma Yates, PI of the Ozone Where We Live (OWWL) project, said: “We have developed an amazing collaboration with Quest Science Center, a non-profit that among many other things supports high school students interested in the Earth’s climate. One of the aspects of Quest is to develop student-run studies by pairing high school students with mentors. OWWL has been working with these students and their Quest mentors to study air quality in the Tri-Valley Region in California (Bay Area into San Joaquin Valley). We designed a mini field campaign over the month of August, with 12 science flights and ground-based sensors at participants’ homes. I know the students (and mentors) would get a kick out of seeing their work highlighted by NASA!” Everyone can join the fun and make a lasting mark on NASA science. You’ll find all our open opportunities at https://science.nasa.gov/citizen-science/ . Happy Thanksgiving! Quest Science Center participants in NASA’s Ozone Where We Live project, from left to right: Rick Stulen, Randy Simpson, Tiffany Nguyen*, Mark Dedon, Pareena Gupta*, Robin Deepak*, Shayan Ghosh*, Rohan Munagapati*, Rahul Eapen*, and Nikhil Madineni*. The students (*) are 11th and 12th graders at Livermore High School in Livermore, CA and Amador High School, in Pleasanton CA.

item.title: Microsoft's official Python agent framework hijacked to distribute malware
item.description: Microsoft’s official agent framework package hosted on PyPI has been hijacked and now installs info-stealing malware, multiple security research firms have discovered. CEO Satya Nadella may be on stage trying to wow investors and customers at his company’s annual Ignite conference , but somewhere in the bowels of a building in Redmond his open source team is likely panicking at what appears to be unauthorized access to an administrator account on Microsoft’s Github organization. The problem package is Microsoft’s agent-framework, versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, researchers reported late yesterday and this morning . According to OX Security, version 1.26.1 was reverted to a safe version, but the attacker later uploaded 1.26.2 through Microsoft’s official PyPI publisher account, suggesting that, at least at the time of their report, the credentials hadn’t been locked down. Safe to say, but if you find either version in your environment assume you have some account security work to do. Microsoft agent-framework for Python boasts nearly 200,000 downloads a month and is used to build and deploy AI agents. As of those latest releases, it’s also being used to exfiltrate environment variables, credential files, and other secrets for Azure, Git, Docker, Hugging Face, and other sensitive developer services. To make matters worse, the package never needs to be imported to do its dirty work – all it takes is a Python interpreter with the package installed to start up – the infected package still pulls the genuine 1.26.0 version of Microsoft’s agent-framework in order to keep itself running and looking legitimate, while in the background it gathers up credentials, encrypts them as a base64-encoded chunk of JSON, and sends them off to a webhook.site address hard coded into the malware. It appears from researcher accounts that this is made to act fast, as the malware isn’t persistent and only runs as long as the malicious version of the agent-framework remains in a site-packages directory. What it does do, however, is not just look for credentials in the environment: It actually starts calling for new ones and collecting them, too. In particular, the malware requests fresh identity tokens from GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps, and Azure itself, which are exfiltrated to the same webhook site. “That combination of passive theft and active token requests makes it especially dangerous in cloud build environments, because even short-lived tokens are useful when they're exfiltrated right away,” said researchers at OpenSourceMalware. The agent-framework GitHub repo is offline as of writing. It’s been pointed out online that Microsoft’s repo for ONNX Runtime , an AI accelerator, is also offline. Other Microsoft repos remain available, and neither Microsoft nor security researchers have linked the ONNX repo’s pull to the malware campaign. “We have made some repositories private while we investigate malicious content,” a Microsoft spokesperson told The Register. “Our priority is

Other Microsoft repos remain available, and neither Microsoft nor security researchers have linked the ONNX repo’s pull to the malware campaign. “We have made some repositories private while we investigate malicious content,” a Microsoft spokesperson told The Register. “Our priority is to protect customers and the broader ecosystem. We are working to review and will take further action as needed.”® Updated at 1805 with comment from Microsoft.

item.title: MongoDB snaps up Firebolt to bring transactions and analytics under one roof
item.description: MongoDB has acquired analytical database specialist Firebolt in another attempt to bring transactional and analytical workloads onto one platform. The document database vendor carved out its patch of the database market with flexible, JSON-like documents rather than rigid, predefined table structures. Developers put it to work in web, mobile, ecommerce, and content management applications. It has since branched out to offer a data platform it says is ready for the age of AI and AI agents working across transactional environments, promising scale, speed and reliability. Firebolt was founded in Israel in 2019. It built a cloud-native data warehouse based on the notion of automatically and transparently merging and compacting files as they are ingested. Speaking to The Register in 2020 , then CTO Eldad Farkash claimed this slashes the amount of data users need to load into the system, accelerating query performance and improving concurrency. Firebolt raised $100 million in Series C funding in 2022 at a reported valuation of $1.4 billion. MongoDB has not disclosed the acquisition price. But what will it get, and what does that mean for MongoDB users? In a blog post , the company said: "By integrating Firebolt into MongoDB's Intelligent Data Platform, we're bringing a high-performance analytics engine to where your operational data already lives. Firebolt's engine will run right alongside your database, and we'll keep it in sync automatically, so there's no pipeline to build or manage. You'll get one platform for operational and real-time analytical workloads, so teams can ship faster, with fewer systems to operate and secure." The integration isn't available yet. MongoDB says customers will gain access in the coming months, while existing Firebolt customers will retain their current service and support. MongoDB's pitch is that AI agents will need fresh operational data and fast analytical answers, without customers having to stitch separate platforms together. MongoDB is hardly the first vendor to chase that combination. Bringing online transaction processing (OLTP) and online analytical processing (OLAP) together promises less infrastructure to manage and fewer data pipelines to maintain. Delivering both without compromises is the harder part. Earlier this year, Databricks claimed to have cracked the problem , promising "one data, zero compromises, zero copies." It works with Reyden – a new compute engine – and Lakebase, its serverless PostgreSQL on open object storage. Rivals pointed out there were briefly two copies of the data in the system at some level. SingleStore also tackles the problem with an in-memory row store and an on-disk column store with tiered storage, "meaning transactions hit memory first, and then they roll off to disk storage," allowing analytics and transactions on a single system. Oracle and SAP have also spent years adding analytical capabilities to transactional platforms to reduce the delay between recording data and analy
item.dc:creator: Lindsay Clark
item.content:encoded: MongoDB has acquired analytical database specialist Firebolt in another attempt to bring transactional and analytical workloads onto one platform. The document database vendor carved out its patch of the database market with flexible, JSON-like documents rather than rigid, predefined table structures. Developers put it to work in web, mobile, ecommerce, and content management applications. It has since branched out to offer a data platform it says is ready for the age of AI and AI agents working across transactional environments, promising scale, speed and reliability. Firebolt was founded in Israel in 2019. It built a cloud-native data warehouse based on the notion of automatically and transparently merging and compacting files as they are ingested. Speaking to The Register in 2020 , then CTO Eldad Farkash claimed this slashes the amount of data users need to load into the system, accelerating query performance and improving concurrency. Firebolt raised $100 million in Series C funding in 2022 at a reported valuation of $1.4 billion. MongoDB has not disclosed the acquisition price. But what will it get, and what does that mean for MongoDB users? In a blog post , the company said: "By integrating Firebolt into MongoDB's Intelligent Data Platform, we're bringing a high-performance analytics engine to where your operational data already lives. Firebolt's engine will run right alongside your database, and we'll keep it in sync automatically, so there's no pipeline to build or manage. You'll get one platform for operational and real-time analytical workloads, so teams can ship faster, with fewer systems to operate and secure." The integration isn't available yet. MongoDB says customers will gain access in the coming months, while existing Firebolt customers will retain their current service and support. MongoDB's pitch is that AI agents will need fresh operational data and fast analytical answers, without customers having to stitch separate platforms together. MongoDB is hardly the first vendor to chase that combination. Bringing online transaction processing (OLTP) and online analytical processing (OLAP) together promises less infrastructure to manage and fewer data pipelines to maintain. Delivering both without compromises is the harder part. Earlier this year, Databricks claimed to have cracked the problem , promising "one data, zero compromises, zero copies." It works with Reyden – a new compute engine – and Lakebase, its serverless PostgreSQL on open object storage. Rivals pointed out there were briefly two copies of the data in the system at some level. SingleStore also tackles the problem with an in-memory row store and an on-disk column store with tiered storage, "meaning transactions hit memory first, and then they roll off to disk storage," allowing analytics and transactions on a single system. Oracle and SAP have also spent years adding analytical capabilities to transactional platforms to reduce the delay between recording data and analyzing it. MongoDB promises real-time analytics without a customer-managed pipeline. Whether that also means avoiding separate copies of the data is less clear. Automatic synchronization doesn't explain how the information is stored or moved underneath. The Register has asked MongoDB to clarify the architecture. MongoDB has been here before. In 2022, it unveiled columnstore indexing designed to help developers build analytical queries into their applications. The idea was to accelerate those queries without changing the document structure or moving data to another system. Firebolt gives MongoDB another tool for a familiar job: making analytics feel at home beside its operational database. Whether the plumbing lives up to the pitch remains to be seen. ®

item.title: 'A shotgun marriage': Why are NASA's SkyFall Mars helicopters riding on a nuclear rocket?
item.description: null The pace is picking up on building, testing, and plotting out the flight paths for a trio of NASA Ingenuity-class helicopters to investigate Mars after riding there on a nuclear-powered rocket. NASA's Skyfall mission will see those mini-choppers dropped off at Mars by the space agency's Space Reactor-1 Freedom (SR-1) rocket, the first fission nuclear-powered interplanetary spacecraft slated for launch in late 2028. After its cruise phase and initial Mars flyby in 2029, that nuclear carrier craft will make a second Mars approach in the Fall of 2030 to unleash a SkyFall entry capsule outfitted with a fleet of small aerial vehicles that will soar across the Red Planet . But some experts are questioning why NASA is combining two such high-profile missions into one. "It is clear that SkyFall was approved for programmatic or political reasons," said Scott Hubbard, former director of NASA's Ames Research Center and the first Mars Program Director (aka the " Mars Czar ") at NASA Headquarters, told Space.com. "The connection to Space Reactor-1 seems to me to be a bit of a shotgun marriage, a tech-demo piggybacking on another mission as an opening bid for a 'nuclear NASA.'" Shotgun marriage? Hubbard is a retired adjunct professor of aeronautics and astronautics at Stanford University. He is a major voice in shaping Red Planet exploration goals, drawing upon his expertise as NASA's former foremost Mars authority. His understanding is that the basic concept had been developed as a follow on to Ingenuity, an attempt to move beyond a technology demo and into a science platform. Hubbard said that combining these two observations, the outcome presents "an unusual set of management issues." Since the SkyFall mission concept first appeared, he said, the usual sequence for a science mission is reversed. "The science community is having to scramble to back into a set of requirements and objectives that match the SkyFall capabilities. Fortunately the community is very creative," said Hubbard, "and the basic Planetary Decadal objectives are very broad." Decadal surveys reflect a broad consensus within the scientific community and provide detailed insights into the strategic priorities and mission directives set for the next decade across key scientific domains, including planetary exploration. Lemonade squeeze However, Hubbard said he has heard griping about the "fait accompli" process, "but the planetary community will make lemonade." It should be noted however, Hubbard continued, that this process is not how you would design a strategic set of missions as precursors for human exploration. "SR-1 Freedom is a technology demo that may or may not be ready for the Mars launch window in 2028. It is clear that the Mars Program has a standard launch concept in their back pocket," said Hubbard. item.dc:creator: Leonard David
item.content:encoded: null The pace is picking up on building, testing, and plotting out the flight paths for a trio of NASA Ingenuity-class helicopters to investigate Mars after riding there on a nuclear-powered rocket. NASA's Skyfall mission will see those mini-choppers dropped off at Mars by the space agency's Space Reactor-1 Freedom (SR-1) rocket, the first fission nuclear-powered interplanetary spacecraft slated for launch in late 2028. After its cruise phase and initial Mars flyby in 2029, that nuclear carrier craft will make a second Mars approach in the Fall of 2030 to unleash a SkyFall entry capsule outfitted with a fleet of small aerial vehicles that will soar across the Red Planet . But some experts are questioning why NASA is combining two such high-profile missions into one. "It is clear that SkyFall was approved for programmatic or political reasons," said Scott Hubbard, former director of NASA's Ames Research Center and the first Mars Program Director (aka the " Mars Czar ") at NASA Headquarters, told Space.com. "The connection to Space Reactor-1 seems to me to be a bit of a shotgun marriage, a tech-demo piggybacking on another mission as an opening bid for a 'nuclear NASA.'" Shotgun marriage? Hubbard is a retired adjunct professor of aeronautics and astronautics at Stanford University. He is a major voice in shaping Red Planet exploration goals, drawing upon his expertise as NASA's former foremost Mars authority. His understanding is that the basic concept had been developed as a follow on to Ingenuity, an attempt to move beyond a technology demo and into a science platform. Hubbard said that combining these two observations, the outcome presents "an unusual set of management issues." Since the SkyFall mission concept first appeared, he said, the usual sequence for a science mission is reversed. "The science community is having to scramble to back into a set of requirements and objectives that match the SkyFall capabilities. Fortunately the community is very creative," said Hubbard, "and the basic Planetary Decadal objectives are very broad." Decadal surveys reflect a broad consensus within the scientific community and provide detailed insights into the strategic priorities and mission directives set for the next decade across key scientific domains, including planetary exploration. Lemonade squeeze However, Hubbard said he has heard griping about the "fait accompli" process, "but the planetary community will make lemonade." It should be noted however, Hubbard continued, that this process is not how you would design a strategic set of missions as precursors for human exploration. "SR-1 Freedom is a technology demo that may or may not be ready for the Mars launch window in 2028. It is clear that the Mars Program has a standard launch concept in their back pocket," said Hubbard. "Nuclear Electric Propulsion [NEP] is of little value in traveling to Mars, not shaving any time off the transit. The real value of NEP is for risk reduction, use at the moon, outer planets and even bolder ideas like interstellar travel," Hubbard concluded. Resolution gap "This, by far, is the shortest Mars mission ever conceived of," said Matthew Golombek, SkyFall Project Scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif., speaking Nov. 10 during the virtual meeting of the Mars Exploration Program Analysis Group (MEPAG). Kick-started by NASA in March 2026, the SkyFall project has grown from roughly six people to over 200 individuals who are now working on the initiative, said Golombek. "This is an incredibly rapid development and build," he said. "It's really to demonstrate that exploration is possible with helicopters … filling what I call a 'resolution gap' between orbital information and surface information," Golombek told the MEPAG. Once deployed by a helicopter deployment system, the threesome will spin up their rotors at about a kilometer above the surface of Mars . Then each helicopter lands on its own, ready to undertake flights every other solar day on the Red Planet. On average, a day (labeled as a sol) on Mars lasts 24 hours 39 minutes 35 seconds, from one noon to the next. Individual SkyFall helicopters tote across the Red Planet a suite of micro-devices to probe the subsurface structure of Mars, investigate the geomorphology and geology of surface terrains, scope out the meteorology of the atmosphere and gauge the planet's radiation environment. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) Scientific tasks SkyFall's prime mission is six months, with a one-year goal," Golombek said, and the intent is to arrive in northern spring on Mars, a time where the vehicles are unlikely to encounter dust storms. On the to-do list of NASA level one science requisites are for the helicopters to capture high-resolution imagery, perform a set scientific tasks, and help to prepare for future human exploration of Mars, said Golombek. From their initial landing spots, the whirlybirds could potentially go tens to 100's of kilometers or more in different directions. Identical for all three helicopters, the nominal payload consists of five instruments, plus engineering navigation cameras. That gear can examine the subsurface structure of Mars, the geomorphology and geology of surface terrains, as well as look at the meteorology of the atmosphere and the planet's radiation environment. Star of the show "The real star of the show is ground penetrating radar [GPR] with a flexible antenna," Golombek noted. That ultra-small GPR hardware can look for buried rocks, the layering of the Mars home turf, as well as spot subsurface ice deposits. "If you have this aerial access and the ability to scout ahead," Golombek said, "you would go a long way towards better defining where to go with a rover and what kind of more detailed surface studies to do with subsequent missions." All that said, yet to be plotted out are science-focused traverses for the SkyFall helicopters. But there are early ideas. "The real kicker is that these spacecraft are the smallest landers ever attempted on Mars," said Golombek. "You are looking for a place that virtually has no rocks," he pointed out, a must-have to assure high probability of landing safely. So toss in for good measure low surface slopes, no big craters, a site not overloaded with dust. Flight path of NASA's Space Reactor-1 Freedom illustrates the spacecraft's journey to Mars, including launch, reactor startup, multiple Mars flybys, and deployment of the SkyFall payload during the mission. (Image credit: NASA) Design reference target One early idea is to revisit the crash locales of discarded SkyFall descent hardware – fuel tanks, cruise stage and associated gear – equipment large and heavy enough to survive entry, smack into the Mars landscape and high-speed and generate craters. "So if there is ice at centimeters depth, we would create our own icy impact craters," Golombek said. "We could actually visit them in a time-scale before the ice actually sublimates," he said. Another site getting the eye, albeit deemed a design reference target but considered a "pretty good spot," is within Arcadia Planitia in Mars's northern lowlands. Studies have indicated the presence of substantial volumes of near-surface excess ice there. "There is a vast amount of information to suggest large quantities of regional ice deposits at that location," said Golombek. "This is at least one location that appears to meet all the engineering constraints and would be a potentially safe landing site…virtually no rocks," he advised. In the past, Golombek added, JPL took part in SpaceX-sponsored workshops to look for ice deposits as close to the equator of Mars that could be found. Arcadia Planitia was flagged as superior Starship touchdown terrain. "Most of the landing sites considered for humans have talked about going to places with ice deposits. Ice provides both a consumable as well as fuel to get back off the planet," said Golombek. On-time delivery For

item.title: Vulcan failure caused by inadequate fuel supply to engines, ULA says
item.description: United Launch Alliance said Wednesday that the failure of its Vulcan rocket during a launch on Sunday was caused by inadequate fuel supply. "ULA has completed an initial integrated review of flight data from the Leo 1 launch anomaly that occurred last Sunday," the company said in a statement . "While work remains to determine cause, preliminary indications are that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines." The new information released by ULA confirms reporting from Ars Technica on Tuesday that the rocket's failure was not due to the performance of the vehicle's main engines, which are provided by Blue Origin. Read full article Comments

item.title: Waymo has stopped its robotaxis from driving on the freeway—here’s why
item.description: Waymo is currently restricting its fleet of robotaxis to surface streets after getting into hot water with California over its cars' driving behavior on highways. Specifically, the software tends to drive into construction zones at speed. As first reported by the San Francisco Business Times , this behavior actually drew the ire of California’s DMV earlier this month, which ordered Waymo to stop driving on Californian highways immediately and until it can convince the DMV that its cars no longer “pose an imminent hazard to public safety.” This is not Waymo’s first run-in with this problem. In Arizona, Waymo robotaxis did not recognize ramp closure signs on six occasions in Phoenix in April and entered construction zones. A month later in California, seven Waymo robotaxis entered lanes with active construction. In June, Waymo recalled the almost 3,800 robotaxis capable of highway driving. That problem led Waymo to stick to surface streets only in California after the May incidents until late July, when the robotaxis resumed highway operations. In early July, Waymo told the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration that it began updating the robotaxi software to a version that “improve[s] the recognition of freeway construction zones, more appropriately prioritize[s] construction zones over other freeway hazards, and reduce[s] speed when the AV detects that it may be in a construction zone.” Read full article Comments

item.title: 'Project Hail Mary' is heading back to theaters this December
item.description: null Fist my bump, everyone, because box office smash hit "Project Hail Mary" is heading back to theaters this December. The exceptional sci-fi movie, based on Andy Weir's book, stars Ryan Gosling as Ryland Grace, a middle-school science teacher who becomes key to saving the world. Together with Rocky, an alien he meets along the way, Grace must solve the riddle of the mysterious substance that's causing the sun (and Rocky's star) to die out. Amazon MGM has revealed the return to theaters with a video showcasing the many accolades that the film received. "Project Hail Mary" returns to the big screen on Dec. 11 and will be shown in all formats, including IMAX and 70MM. Ryan Gosling upside down floating in zero gravity in Project Hail Mary (2026). (Image credit: MGM) "Project Hail Mary" was a massive success for Amazon MGM, grossing over $600 million worldwide when it first dropped in theaters back in March 2026. It was also a huge hit with critics, scoring an average of 95% on Rotten Tomatoes , and more importantly, getting two big thumbs up in our review ! Dec. 11 is a smart choice by MGM too, as it puts the sci-fi spectacle back in front of audiences a week ahead of Avengers: Doomsday and Dune: Part 3. That's not a battle you want to get in the middle of. If you missed "Project Hail Mary" in theaters the first time, I'd definitely recommend you try to catch one of these screenings. It's a beautiful movie — visually and emotionally — and it deserves to be seen on the big screen. item.title: The wrong setting for AI cache can cost you a lot of cash
item.description: Be wary of AI costs. You may be spending more than you think and end up with nothing to show for it but an eye-popping invoice. Register readers are finding themselves on the sharp, pointy end of AI billing, confused about which costs are covered by what, and surprised by "features" that burn through credit, seemingly without warning. Startups without the deep pockets of established companies are the first to feel the squeeze. Sometimes, the approach feels more like an app that urges users to deposit extra cash to keep that streak going than a helpful coding assistant. Take one reader, who told The Register about Claude burning through credits at a ferocious rate after a cache setting was reset in the background. The cache setting controlled how long Claude "remembered" requests and was set to one hour. It's a useful feature, and it lets Claude reuse material that has already been processed. Once it expires, continuing unfinished work can mean paying to process old material again. "After hitting my $200 Ultra plan limit," our reader told us, "I bought $250 in additional credits to finish 8 coding threads." There didn't seem to be much work left to do, so the extra credits should have been plenty. Alas, no, after just under two hours, the entire balance was gone, and no meaningful progress was made. They dug deeper and found that the newer request had switched back to the five-minute cache "without my action or knowledge." The figures didn't add up either, so he made a request to Anthropic to explain the cache setting change and the cost discrepancy. "I found myself stuck with its support chatbot, Fin. It described the cache switch behavior as a 'feature' and said it couldn't provide the reconciliation or investigation." The support thread was then closed. Our reader asked again for an explanation. "Fin kept closing the support thread, sometimes just 31 seconds after I asked for human escalation." The Register asked Anthropic for an explanation, and how users might reach a human when a chatbot comes to the end of its usefulness, but the company has yet to respond. It's all a bit of a cautionary tale. Our reader said, "The money was gone, the work was unfinished, and I was spending time chasing answers that I needed to spend building my app. "I wish I'd known this could happen before buying those credits." Indeed. There are endless stories of how using AI has resulted in unexpected costs. Even celebrity mathematician Dr Hannah Fry found the token costs of sending an agent on an errand a surprise. And then there are the misunderstandings when credits gifted under one program turn out to be inapplicable for another, and support teams play a variant of ping-pong , just with customer requests. The problem is that burning through credits or running up bills that could wipe out a start-up is all too easy. We've been here before with the cloud , and it appears the lessons need to be learned again. Our reader complained, "We deserve to understand what we'r

item.title: LG Electronics Brings Smarter, More Connected Living to African Homes
item.description: The role of home appliances is changing. Today’s consumers expect more than products that simply perform everyday tasks. They want solutions that are intuitive, efficient and capable of making daily life easier. Across Africa, rapid urbanisation, changing lifestyles and growing digital adoption are reshaping consumer expectations. Homeowners are increasingly seeking appliances that combine convenience, performance, energy efficiency and intelligent functionality while fitting seamlessly into their everyday routines. In response, LG Electronics continues to develop innovations that place people at the centre of technology. Guided by its vision for smarter, more connected living, the company is introducing solutions that help consumers spend less time on household chores and more time on what matters most. item.title: Cyber insurers now want proof you can actually recover
item.description: Cyber insurance pricing has cooled. Marsh’s Global Insurance Market Index shows global cyber rates falling for a 13th consecutive quarter, with US rates recently stabilizing after the ransomware-driven spikes of 2020 and 2021 . Part of the reason rates are lowering is because carriers are imposing stricter requirements that determine if you will qualify at all. A major global carrier recently stopped writing law firms altogether because of claims volume, and brokers expect healthcare and managed service providers (MSPs) to be next. The newest requirement is the one many MSPs are least ready for: proof that you can actually recover. This is what insurers really want to see, and meeting the bar is harder than it sounds. Why insurers stopped taking backups on faith In a recent webinar with cyber insurance provider Beltex , the familiar list of requirements came up first: Multifactor authentication (MFA) on external access and privileged accounts Endpoint detection and response (EDR) on every endpoint A staffed 24/7 team where managed detection and response (MDR) is required, and timely patching. Backup is now joining that list, and for good reason. For years it was assumed that having backups and a green job status was good enough. Claims have shown otherwise. Now, attackers go after backup infrastructure to make their ransomware more effective, and an untested restore can re-infect the production network. Beltex described an MSP that restored a client directly from backup without involving the insurer. The attackers were still in the environment, and the ransom reportedly doubled. So, carriers are asking for proof. Some want evidence of a successful restore within the last six months, and some insurance applications must be signed by a C-level executive rather than the IT director to put ownership behind it. Proof of speed matters as much as proof of recovery Being able to recover is only half the question, because time is where claim costs balloon. Insurers, it turns out, don’t object to paying claims. They object to paying big ones. Beltex’s favorite example involved an 85-person firm hit through a zero-day firewall flaw. Their MDR solution contained the intrusion in about 20 minutes, forensics confirmed two servers were touched, and clean backups had the firm fully functional within 36 hours. The claim came in at around $85,000. Compare that with downtime and business interruption: a firm billing $10,000 a day that is offline for a week loses $70,000 in income before recovery costs and claim submission. Yet large servers can take four to 24 hours to restore. That is why underwriters care how fast you can come back and how successfully. Where you recover is the other half Speed raises a second problem: where do you restore to? Breach counsel treats the first 72 hours as the most critical window, and incident response (IR) teams need to isolate and investigate infected systems during it. Restoring into production too early risks reintroducing the

item.content:encoded: Cyber insurance pricing has cooled. Marsh’s Global Insurance Market Index shows global cyber rates falling for a 13th consecutive quarter, with US rates recently stabilizing after the ransomware-driven spikes of 2020 and 2021 . Part of the reason rates are lowering is because carriers are imposing stricter requirements that determine if you will qualify at all. A major global carrier recently stopped writing law firms altogether because of claims volume, and brokers expect healthcare and managed service providers (MSPs) to be next. The newest requirement is the one many MSPs are least ready for: proof that you can actually recover. This is what insurers really want to see, and meeting the bar is harder than it sounds. Why insurers stopped taking backups on faith In a recent webinar with cyber insurance provider Beltex , the familiar list of requirements came up first: Multifactor authentication (MFA) on external access and privileged accounts Endpoint detection and response (EDR) on every endpoint A staffed 24/7 team where managed detection and response (MDR) is required, and timely patching. Backup is now joining that list, and for good reason. For years it was assumed that having backups and a green job status was good enough. Claims have shown otherwise. Now, attackers go after backup infrastructure to make their ransomware more effective, and an untested restore can re-infect the production network. Beltex described an MSP that restored a client directly from backup without involving the insurer. The attackers were still in the environment, and the ransom reportedly doubled. So, carriers are asking for proof. Some want evidence of a successful restore within the last six months, and some insurance applications must be signed by a C-level executive rather than the IT director to put ownership behind it. Proof of speed matters as much as proof of recovery Being able to recover is only half the question, because time is where claim costs balloon. Insurers, it turns out, don’t object to paying claims. They object to paying big ones. Beltex’s favorite example involved an 85-person firm hit through a zero-day firewall flaw. Their MDR solution contained the intrusion in about 20 minutes, forensics confirmed two servers were touched, and clean backups had the firm fully functional within 36 hours. The claim came in at around $85,000. Compare that with downtime and business interruption: a firm billing $10,000 a day that is offline for a week loses $70,000 in income before recovery costs and claim submission. Yet large servers can take four to 24 hours to restore. That is why underwriters care how fast you can come back and how successfully. Where you recover is the other half Speed raises a second problem: where do you restore to? Breach counsel treats the first 72 hours as the most critical window, and incident response (IR) teams need to isolate and investigate infected systems during it. Restoring into production too early risks reintroducing the threat and disturbing the evidence investigators need. Waiting for a safe place has the clock running. Recovery that is fast but not safe doesn’t satisfy anyone. Meeting all of this is harder than it looks Put the pieces together and the bar is high: Backups you have actually tested Recovery times you can state and meet And a clean, separate place to recover to Underwriters want to know whether you exercised reasonable care, so a row of green checkmarks won’t do. Run a test restore. Confirm you’re protecting everything that matters, including the server someone labeled “not in production.” Have the business owner, not just IT, confirm the right systems came back within agreed recovery time objectives (RTO) and recovery point objectives (RPO), and keep the logs, screenshots and sign-off in your ticketing system. It doesn’t need to resemble a government audit; Beltex noted that this alone puts you ahead of most organizations. Where cloud disaster recovery fits Cloud-native disaster recovery changes the equation. Cove’s DRaaS solution lets teams stage a pre-recovered VM in the N-able cloud that can be failed over to in about 15 minutes, off the production network. That answers the speed question and the location question together. Forensic investigators can validate and hunt in the sandbox while the business keeps moving, with rollback to earlier points in time. Once everyone agrees the recovery point is clean, workloads can run from the cloud over VPN, and failback uses recovery agents to bring changes home. Where to start Insurance is a financial failsafe, not a substitute for a bad data protection posture. Start by listing what the business couldn’t lose for 72 hours, set recovery targets, test them and document the results. Check the policy itself: a standalone cyber policy rather than a small add-on to a general one, with a limit of at least $1 million, and $2 million as the business scales. And if an incident does hit, disconnect affected machines from the network rather than powering them off, so forensic data survives. N-able Cove Data Protection, recognized as a Champion in the Infotech 2026 Enterprise Backup Data Quadrant, provides cloud-native data protection for organizations. Learn more at n-able.com/products/cove-data-protection . Contributed by N-able.

item.title: NASA Data Clinches First-of-Its-Kind Stellar Merger
item.description: Explore Webb Science James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) NASA Data Clinches… Webb News Latest News Latest Images Webb’s Blog Awards X (offsite – login reqd) Instagram (offsite – login reqd) Facebook (offsite- login reqd) Youtube (offsite) Overview About Who is James Webb? Fact Sheet Impacts+Benefits FAQ Webb Timeline Science Overview and Goals Early Universe Galaxies Over Time Star Lifecycle Other Worlds Science/Engineering Explainers Observatory Overview Launch Deployment Orbit Mirrors Sunshield Instruments & ISIM Module Instrument: NIRCam Instrument: MIRI Instrument: NIRSpec Instrument: FGS/NIRISS Optical Telescope Element Backplane Spacecraft Bus Webb vs Hubble -> Multimedia About Webb Images Images Videos Products & Activities Podcasts Webb Image Sonifications What is Webb Observing? 3d Webb in 3d Solar System Webb’s First Images Team International Team People Of Webb More For the Media For Scientists For Educators For Fun/Learning 7 Min Read NASA Data Clinches First-of-Its-Kind Stellar Merger In December 2025, observations from NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope provided the final evidence that allowed researchers to fully reconstruct what happened before, during, and after the merger of a binary star system nicknamed Bao in the Andromeda galaxy. Credits: Image: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Viraj Karambelkar (Columbia), Kishalay De (Columbia); Image Processing: Alyssa Pagan (STScI); Acknowledgment: DSS, Robert Gendler Researchers recently identified a first of its kind: A star slightly less massive than the Sun spiraled into and merged with a puffy supergiant star at the outskirts of our neighboring Andromeda galaxy. They nicknamed the newly single, potentially “rejuvenated” star Bao. Their NASA-funded discovery was then bolstered by quick-turn observations from NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope that were carefully cross-referenced with extensive data from telescopes in space and on the ground. “Stellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict,” said Viraj Karambelkar, the first author of a new paper in Nature published Wednesday and a NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University in New York. “However, we noticed something unusual was going on in 2023 and continued to monitor the system to see what it would do. Then, in 2025, it erupted! Webb observed Bao only 47 days after the stars’ eruption peaked, the earliest ever follow-up of an event like this. The telescope’s data helped us characterize what the system looked like before, during, and immediately after the merger, which is absolutely mind-blowing.” Image: AT 2025abao in the Andromeda Galaxy In December 2025, observations from NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope provided the final evidence that allowed researchers to fully reconstruct what happened before, during, and after the merger of a binary star system nicknamed Bao in the Andromeda galaxy. Image: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Viraj Karambelkar (Columbia), Kishalay De (Columbia); Image Processing: Alys

Fact Sheet Impacts+Benefits FAQ Webb Timeline Science Overview and Goals Early Universe Galaxies Over Time Star Lifecycle Other Worlds Science/Engineering Explainers Observatory Overview Launch Deployment Orbit Mirrors Sunshield Instruments & ISIM Module Instrument: NIRCam Instrument: MIRI Instrument: NIRSpec Instrument: FGS/NIRISS Optical Telescope Element Backplane Spacecraft Bus Webb vs Hubble -> Multimedia About Webb Images Images Videos Products & Activities Podcasts Webb Image Sonifications What is Webb Observing? 3d Webb in 3d Solar System Webb’s First Images Team International Team People Of Webb More For the Media For Scientists For Educators For Fun/Learning 7 Min Read NASA Data Clinches First-of-Its-Kind Stellar Merger In December 2025, observations from NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope provided the final evidence that allowed researchers to fully reconstruct what happened before, during, and after the merger of a binary star system nicknamed Bao in the Andromeda galaxy. Credits: Image: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Viraj Karambelkar (Columbia), Kishalay De (Columbia); Image Processing: Alyssa Pagan (STScI); Acknowledgment: DSS, Robert Gendler Researchers recently identified a first of its kind: A star slightly less massive than the Sun spiraled into and merged with a puffy supergiant star at the outskirts of our neighboring Andromeda galaxy. They nicknamed the newly single, potentially “rejuvenated” star Bao. Their NASA-funded discovery was then bolstered by quick-turn observations from NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope that were carefully cross-referenced with extensive data from telescopes in space and on the ground. “Stellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict,” said Viraj Karambelkar, the first author of a new paper in Nature published Wednesday and a NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University in New York. “However, we noticed something unusual was going on in 2023 and continued to monitor the system to see what it would do. Then, in 2025, it erupted! Webb observed Bao only 47 days after the stars’ eruption peaked, the earliest ever follow-up of an event like this. The telescope’s data helped us characterize what the system looked like before, during, and immediately after the merger, which is absolutely mind-blowing.” Image: AT 2025abao in the Andromeda Galaxy In December 2025, observations from NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope provided the final evidence that allowed researchers to fully reconstruct what happened before, during, and after the merger of a binary star system nicknamed Bao in the Andromeda galaxy. Image: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Viraj Karambelkar (Columbia), Kishalay De (Columbia); Image Processing: Alyssa Pagan (STScI); Acknowledgment: DSS, Robert Gendler Before their transformation, the two stars spent millennia placidly orbiting one another as a binary pair. But once the smaller star came into contact with the surface of the giant star, their “unification” happened after only seven orbits (about seven years). Other known binary star mergers, featuring two smaller stars, occurred after thousands of orbits. “We thought an outburst from a such an extended star would take years,” said co-author Nadia Blagorodnova, an associate professor at the University of Barcelona in Spain. “One day, its brightness started rising and within a week, it peaked!” “When a companion star begins to interact with the outer surface of the primary star, it produces a subtle effect — a slow brightening, which we clearly saw in Bao’s data,” said co-author Kishalay De, an assistant professor at Columbia University in New York. “As the companion continues its orbit, it keeps peeling off the primary star’s outer layers, and that gas flows away into the surrounding space.” This is the beginning of a high-stakes showdown some binary stars go through, known as a common envelope evolution. The gas between the stars at this stage is known as a common envelope because its outer layer is shared between them. In this system, the primary star engulfed the smaller star and the companion plummeted, spiraling through the envelope as it was robbed of orbital energy by drag. While Webb’s data proved the stars merged, a merger wasn’t the only possible outcome for this system. In other systems, both stars survive the process — shedding a lot of mass along the way, but remaining independent in tight orbits. Over time, such surviving pairs can transform into neutron stars and black holes , explode as supernovae , produce ripples in space-time known as gravitational waves , and create millisecond pulsars . Hitting “replay” The team reconstructed what happened to Bao by updating their ongoing simulations. They found the model that matched Webb’s mid-infrared observations, which detailed the dust shed by the more massive primary star over centuries. The team concluded that prior to the eruption, Bao’s primary star dwarfed the Sun: It was seven times as massive, 350 times the radius, and 18,000 times brighter — making “Big Bao” an appropriate nickname. “It was an absolute beast of a star, completely outshining its companion in the data,” said co-author Karel Temmink, a Ph.D. student at Radboud University in Nijmegen, Netherlands, who led the simulations. Their modeling resulted in the first mass estimate for the smaller, now demolished, companion. Compared to our Sun, they found that “Little Bao” was likely less massive (about 0.7 solar masses), with a slightly smaller radius and fainter. After revealing the masses of the pair, the model showed there might be leftover energy for Little Bao to “flee” the scene. However, further analysis determined that Little Bao was dragged into Big Bao’s core. Their encounter was “almost like a bomb exploding inside a living star,” De said. What does the new star — now simply Bao — look like today? Only future observations will identify how its “heft” settles. Image: Andromeda Star Merger (Artist’s Concept) Top to bottom, left to right: In this artist’s concept, the stars are surrounded by a dust shell pre-merger; the stars brightened and the companion star’s orbit began to slow as the larger star engulfed it; the eruption occurred; dust freely expands at the poles after the merger. Illustration: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Leah Hustak (STScI); Science: Viraj Karambelkar (Columbia) Reconstructing what happened While Webb’s data allowed the team to measure how much mass was ejected during this process and how efficient the process of common envelope evolution was, Karambelkar’s team also used observations that span ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared light from several telescopes to watch the events, often as they unfolded. (In fact, they published their first paper right before the eruption in 2025.) Bao first caught the team’s attention in February 2023, when they saw an unusual variable star in data from NASA’s retired NEOWISE (Near-Earth Object Wide-Field Infrared Survey Explorer) mission. Before 2018, the object had a consistent luminosity. Observations from the Wide-field Infrared Transient Explorer (WINTER) in September 2024 showed that Bao was not only beginning to brighten, but also spew dust. When NASA’s SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer) serendipitously saw Bao fade rapidly in visible light and brighten in infrared light during a routine survey in July 2025, the researchers knew it was an indicator of unusual activity. The Zwicky Transient Facility detected the eruption on Oct. 17, 2025, watching the stars rapidly brighten and radically heat up. In November 2025, the team received fast-turn observations fro

item.title: How M.C. Escher’s Art Creates Bizarre Mathematical Worlds
item.description: Maurits Cornelis Escher didn’t plan on becoming the darling of mathematicians. Born in 1898 in the canal-lined city of Leeuwarden in the Netherlands, Escher struggled with mathematics as a student, once remarking that he “never got a pass mark.” He ended up studying decorative arts and printmaking, and he used his artwork to explore the strange rules of nature that he found operating around him. Source

item.title: PowerShell 7 heading into Windows as 5.1 hits the end of the road
item.description: Microsoft has confirmed that, at long last, PowerShell 7 will come bundled with Windows, while the venerable PowerShell 5.1 begins its long retirement. It has been a long time coming, although PowerShell 5.1 isn't going away immediately. It will, however, " be removed from a future version of Windows ," and Windows Server 2025 and Windows 11 26H2 are the last versions to include PowerShell 5.1 enabled by default. After that, PowerShell 5.1 will be available as a Feature On Demand (FOD) before eventually shuffling off into the sunset, while PowerShell 7 takes over automation duties. PowerShell 5.1 is now more than ten years old and runs on the .NET Framework. PowerShell 7 is its cross-platform, open source successor, but compatibility isn't seamless. PowerShell was the brainchild of Jeffrey Snover , who sought to bring script automation to Windows at a time when graphical user interfaces were king. He recalled executives telling him "admins don't want command line interfaces," and "exactly what part of effing Windows is confusing you?" but eventually won the argument, and we reckon countless Windows administrators owe him a debt of gratitude. PowerShell 5.1 hasn't had many new features for years. "PowerShell 7 is the modern PowerShell: the one we develop in the open, across platforms, and where new features go," wrote Jason Helmick, a senior product manager on Microsoft's PowerShell team. But compatibility niggles remain. The two can run side by side, so existing scripts won't have to move immediately. Finding and testing everything scattered across an enterprise estate, however, could keep administrators occupied for some time. Microsoft also has unfinished work on the bundled version's MSIX packaging, including support for running as SYSTEM, DISM cmdlets, and machine-wide settings. Those gaps matter for scheduled tasks, services, and management scripts. Despite the deprecation, PowerShell 5.1 will continue to receive updates based on the lifecycle of the Windows version on which it runs. It will eventually be removed based on usage data and "communicated in advance," according to Microsoft. Administrators have time to prepare, but checking which scripts run unchanged, which need work, and which still depend on 5.1 won't happen by itself. "Including PowerShell 7 in Windows is a milestone we've been working toward since PowerShell went cross-platform," Helmick wrote, although the bundled release is still ahead. Microsoft says PowerShell 7 will arrive with the next Windows release, but hasn't named it. 27H2, anyone? ®

item.title: AI-powered cyber threats are changing the rules of enterprise recovery
item.description: Cybersecurity has long been a contest between attackers finding new ways in and defenders trying to keep them out. Artificial intelligence is making that contest more complicated, giving cybercriminals new ways to develop and adapt their attacks while putting additional pressure on conventional cyber defences. For enterprise IT leaders, the challenge extends beyond preventing a breach. What happens when an attacker gets through? Can compromised data be identified, clean copies recovered, and essential systems brought back online without prolonged disruption? These questions are becoming increasingly important as organizations confront both traditional threats and emerging AI-powered cyberattacks. A successful defense strategy must, therefore, account for what happens after an incident, not just the measures designed to prevent one. Making recovery part of the defence This is where cyber-resilient enterprise storage has an important role to play. Rather than relying solely on traditional backup processes, organizations need ways to protect critical data, detect potential compromise, establish which copies can safely be recovered, and restore those copies as quickly as possible. Infinidat addresses this challenge through its InfiniBox and InfiniBox SSA enterprise storage platforms, which incorporate the company’s InfiniSafe cyber resilience and recovery software suite. InfiniSafe combines immutable snapshots, which cannot be altered or deleted during their protected retention period, with logical air-gapping to isolate the management plane from the data plane. Fenced forensic environments provide a separate space for validating data before recovery. The technology also supports automated cyber protection, allowing security monitoring data center wide cyber security software applications or a Security Operations Center (SOC) to automatically talk to InfiniBoxes and trigger immutable snapshots when suspicious activity is detected. This helps reduce the window in which critical data might be exposed. For organizations concerned about recovering compromised information, optional InfiniSafe Cyber Detection uses AI-based analysis to help identify cyber affected data and locate the last known good copy of the data for recovery. Speed is another consideration. Infinidat guarantees recovery of immutable snapshots in one minute or less for InfiniBox and InfiniBox SSA, subject to the guarantee’s terms and conditions. Ultimately, cyber resilience isn’t about assuming every cyberattack can be stopped. It’s about ensuring that when defences are breached, organizations have the tools and processes to recover trusted data and limit the operational consequences. For enterprise IT teams, that makes recovery readiness an essential part of the cybersecurity conversation. Sponsored by Infinidat

item.title: Supernova explodes before astronomers' eyes | Space photo of the day for Nov. 18, 2026
item.description: null Before-and-after photos showing the appearance of a new supernova designated SN 2026ahvu. (Image credit: Dark Energy Survey/DOE/FNAL/DECam/CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/. Acknowledgment: PIs: G. Narayan & T. Murphey (University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign) Image processing: M. Zamani & D. de Martin (NSF NOIRLab)) A new supernova has been spotted exploding in the spiral galaxy NGC 1433, about 50 million light-years from Earth. What is it? Researchers have discovered a new supernova called SN 2026ahvu. A Type Ia supernova, this event took place in a system with two stars orbiting one another (also known as a binary system), in which typically one star is an exploding white dwarf . During most type Ia supernovae, the white dwarf pulls material away from the other star until enough accumulates on its surface to create an explosion. Finding galaxies where stellar explosions are taking place isn't a rarity. However, this supernova is unique in how early it was captured. If the supernova were starting to dim, researchers might infer that the event was ending. However, according to details shared when it was first spotted, as well as later observations, this supernova was discovered while getting brighter. This indicates that the supernova was likely caught early in the process of exploding, providing researchers with a unique opportunity to observe the event as it is taking place. By exploring observations of the galaxy before, during and (in the future) after the supernova event, researchers can investigate this type Ia supernova and how it affected the system in which it took place. Why is it incredible? Scientists made this discovery using ATLAS, or the Asteroid Terrestrial-impact System, which is a robotic astronomical survey made up of telescopes across both hemispheres. ATLAS is designed to spot incoming near-Earth objects like asteroids before they can reach Earth. It's essentially an asteroid impact early warning system. But just because that's what the system is designed for doesn't mean that's all it can do. The system can also spot other objects moving through space and, in this instance, it was able to capture observations of this supernova. Following its initial discovery, other observations of the supernova were made using NOIRLab's Dark Energy Camera (DECam) and Gemini South telescope.

item.title: Space robot legend Voyager 1 is now more than 1 light-day away
item.description: NASA's Voyager 1 probe is now more than one light-day from Earth – so distant that a radio signal takes 24 hours to reach it. The veteran spacecraft has spent almost 50 years getting there. Voyager 1 was launched on September 5, 1977, from Cape Canaveral in Florida. Planning for the mission began in the 1960s, while NASA was working feverishly to put a man on the Moon ahead of the Soviet Union. A rare alignment of the outer planets made a tour of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune possible. Voyager 2 eventually visited all four; Voyager 1's route prioritized Saturn's moon Titan, ruling out a subsequent encounter with Pluto. Voyager 1 completed a flyby of Jupiter in 1979, and passed Saturn and Titan in 1980. Its final imaging sequence in 1990 produced the solar system "Family Portrait," including the famous Pale Blue Dot image of Earth. The cameras were then switched off for good. Thirty-six years after those final pictures, Voyager 1 remains in contact with Earth, with two science instruments still operating: the magnetometer and plasma wave subsystem. Others have been shut down over the decades to conserve the dwindling power supplied by its radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs). Dr Garry Hunt, a member of Voyager's original imaging team, told The Register : "Voyager's real success is the way it used reliable equipment. Well-tested Mariner equipment, and special new things that had come about for it. "We had fault protection on board as well. If anything goes wrong, it automatically switches to a backup. So there was always a backup. There was always a safe mode. We had to have radiation protection on board … when we designed this, we didn't really know the magnetic environment around Jupiter, and to be told it was so strong, 1,000 times stronger than we anticipated, really threw everything up in the air, and so that had to be dealt with." Hunt paid tribute to the succession of project managers and engineers who have kept the probe running over the years. "I think this was a really wonderful example of project management, of clever management of engineering, and interesting science coming out of it, which has made history books and gone to be a catalyst for other things in the future," he said. Voyager 1 may now take two days to answer a call from Earth. After almost 50 years, the remarkable thing is that it still answers at all. ®

item.title: StubHub International warns customer data may have left the venue
item.description: Ticket resale giant StubHub International has warned customers that a recent breach may have exposed their personal information to cybercriminals. The company said it detected "unauthorized access to certain systems" on its platform between late October and early November. Customer notification emails seen by The Register list potentially affected information including names, email addresses, phone numbers, and country or regional settings. StubHub International, operated by Ticketbis S.L., apologized for the intrusion and offered the usual promise to implement security enhancements after the fact. The company said it had addressed "certain vulnerabilities" while containing the incident and was continuing to monitor for suspicious activity. Outside cybersecurity experts are assisting with the ongoing investigation. The company warned that any exposed information could be used to make subsequent scams more convincing. "To date, we have found no evidence of unauthorised access to account passwords , banking information or payment card details," the email stated. "We also have no evidence that the compromised information has been used fraudulently. "However, there is a risk that third parties could use this information to attempt fraud, identity theft or phishing through emails, messages or calls that appear to come from StubHub International or other trusted organizations." The Register contacted StubHub International for more information, such as how many customers were affected, but it did not respond. Digital Fuel Capital bought StubHub International from Viagogo in 2021 after the UK's Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) required the international business to be sold to address competition concerns. In June, the CMA fined Ticketbis £889,200 and ordered refunds exceeding £590,000 after finding that mandatory fees were omitted from upfront ticket prices. StubHub International also recently faced criticism for allowing a single ticket tout to advertise £1 million worth of U2 tickets, despite its stated opposition to ticket-buying bots. ®

item.title: The Lego Star Trek bridge diorama set should be your gateway to finally watching the Original Series
item.description: null It's not quite a five-year mission, but as Star Trek celebrated its 60th anniversary in September of this year (we may have mentioned it once or twice), I decided it was high time I finally watched the original Star Trek . Before this year, I hadn't seen a single episode of "Star Trek: The Original Series", as it's now known. I'm a millennial; I grew up on "The Next Generation", "Deep Space Nine" and "Voyager". By comparison, the old series (TOS) always looked so… old and naff whenever I saw clips of it. But now I have seen the original series. Over the course of 2026, I've ploughed through all 79 episodes, spread across three seasons. And you know what? It's pretty damn good. Even with the shiny 2006 remasters, you'll have to prepare yourself for some bad special effects work, but the scripts are interesting, the sci-fi concepts are out there, and the acting — especially from Shatner and Nimoy — is top-notch. And just as I finally discovered a love for this classic sci-fi series, what should drop into my lap? Why it's the new Star Trek: U.S.S. Enterprise NCC-1701 Bridge diorama set from Lego. Now I have more on my wishlist to add to the Best lego space sets. Boldly building where no one has built before Building the Lego Star Trek: Bridge diorama. Still, that's no small investment for a toy, even if it will make a lovely display piece when it's built. item.dc:creator: Ian Stokes
item.content:encoded: null It's not quite a five-year mission, but as Star Trek celebrated its 60th anniversary in September of this year (we may have mentioned it once or twice), I decided it was high time I finally watched the original Star Trek . Before this year, I hadn't seen a single episode of "Star Trek: The Original Series", as it's now known. I'm a millennial; I grew up on "The Next Generation", "Deep Space Nine" and "Voyager". By comparison, the old series (TOS) always looked so… old and naff whenever I saw clips of it. But now I have seen the original series. Over the course of 2026, I've ploughed through all 79 episodes, spread across three seasons. And you know what? It's pretty damn good. Even with the shiny 2006 remasters, you'll have to prepare yourself for some bad special effects work, but the scripts are interesting, the sci-fi concepts are out there, and the acting — especially from Shatner and Nimoy — is top-notch. And just as I finally discovered a love for this classic sci-fi series, what should drop into my lap? Why it's the new Star Trek: U.S.S. Enterprise NCC-1701 Bridge diorama set from Lego. Now I have more on my wishlist to add to the Best lego space sets. Boldly building where no one has built before Building the Lego Star Trek: Bridge diorama. (Image credit: Future (Ian Stokes)) Let's start with the Band-Aid rip: this set is $200. I know; it stings, especially when Star Trek promised us a future where money doesn't exist. But at 1701 pieces (nice, I see what you did there), it's much better value from a bricks-per-dollar perspective than the X-Files set we checked out recently. Still, that's no small investment for a toy, even if it will make a lovely display piece when it's built. As the name suggests, you get a full Lego-ified recreation of the bridge of the USS Enterprise (NCC-1701, no A, B, C, or D). This includes Captain Kirk's chair, the helm positions ahead of him (manned by Chekov and Sulu), and all of the surrounding computer displays where you usually find Spock, Uhura and Scotty. There's even a viewscreen that can sit in front of the crew, displaying an adorable Klingon commander facing off against Kirk. The minifigure bridge crew of the U.S.S. Enterprise (L-R): Nurse Chapel, Chekov, Scotty, Spock, Kirk, McCoy, Uhura and Sulu. (Image credit: Future (Ian Stokes)) Star Trek: U.S.S. Enterprise NCC-1701 Bridge: $199.99 Board the legendary starship and meet the crew of the U.S.S. Enterprise NCC-1701 for an amazing building experience. Recreate the iconic bridge and transporter room that served as the backdrop for epic scenes from "Star Trek: The Original Series". View Deal Alongside the main bridge, there are a few fun extras bolted on, including a rotating transporter pad (which can make minifigures "disappear") and a working turbolift door connected to the back of the main bridge diorama. You'll have to make the swoosh sound effect yourself, though. It's a wonderfully faithful recreation of Kirk's command center, complete with computer panels and screens, swiveling chairs and that weird scope thing that Spock was always looking into. That said, it's a little lacking in proper Easter eggs. There are some tribbles hiding around the build, and the monitors have custom stickers showing cool Trekkie things. The weapon display racks on the back hold an array of pointy Klingon blades, Starfleet phasers, Sulu's fencing rapier and even Spock's harp, but compared to, say, the X-Files set we built recently, it feels a bit lacking in those deep-cut references. Helping Star Trek live long and prosper The complete Lego Star Trek: U.S.S. Enterprise NCC-1701 Bridge diorama (Image credit: Future (Ian Stokes)) All in all, it's a fantastic little diorama, but when it was announced, I'll admit I was a little puzzled as to who it was aimed at. "Star Trek fans, duh!" is the obvious response, but the Venn diagram crossover between "people who are nostalgic for the original series of Star Trek" and "people who want to buy $200 Lego sets" has to be pretty small, right? Star Trek first aired way back in 1966, which means the first generation of fans are now 70 years old and upwards. Lord knows I hope I'm still building Lego sets when I'm 70, but is that a large enough crowd to make this set a success? Then again the show was repeated and syndicated throughout the 70s and 80s, which means hopefully there'll be some younger buyers, too. The playset aspects of the set are even more puzzling. The working door, exploding monitor and spinning transporter pad are great additions to a kids' playset, but this isn't that — it's a display for nostalgic Star Trek fans. The design of the set just feels a bit confused. Scotty minifigure on the transporter pad. (Image credit: Future (Ian Stokes)) But then it hit me. Maybe this isn't just for fans of the original series; maybe it's meant to create some new fans. I started watching the original Star Trek 60 years after its debut because… well, I'm the sci-fi editor for a space website, and it felt wrong that I hadn't seen it. But most people don't have that sort of professional impetus. The average person won't jump back to watch a 60-year-old TV show without a polite nudge, and this set does a great job of highlighting the charm and optimism of Star Trek's debut outing. I don't know, maybe I'm just projecting here. Maybe Lego bought the rights to make Star Trek sets and needed something to do after they'd mined all the nostalgia they could from the excellent Enterprise D set they released in 2025. Maybe this is just a toy for big kids. Or maybe… just maybe, it's meant to inspire the next generation of Star Trek fans to check out where the magic started. Disclaimer: We were sent a copy of the Star Trek: U.S.S. Enterprise NCC-1701 Bridge set by Lego.

item.title: Tesla’s $30,000 Cybercab comes with a $299 monthly catch
item.description: There is always a catch. Or in the case of Tesla ’s self-driving Cybercab , several. Last Friday night, Tesla said it had invited “select customers” to purchase their very own Cybercabs. The two-seat, gold vehicle is unlike any other on the market: It lacks a steering wheel and brake pedals, and is primarily driven by software. (Other autonomous vehicle companies, including Alphabet's Waymo and Amazon’s Zoox , offer self-driving rides on ride-hail networks , but don’t let people buy their cars.) Tesla’s " limited release ” will supposedly offer some people (unclear how many) the opportunity to pay $29,900 to take delivery in December. From there, though, the Cybercab will need constant cash infusions to stay on the road. Read full article Comments

item.title: Business as usual, but Huang ain't coming back, says Nvidia
item.description: Nvidia's board says it has no plans to bring Jensen Huang back as the GPU giant reports quarterly revenue more than double that of a year ago. The AI infrastructure leviathan had some reassuring to do after its leather-jacketed rockstar leader left under a cloud last week. Huang had been central to its rise as the dominant supplier of AI compute. Newly appointed board chair Harvey Jones ruled out an imminent comeback, saying: "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." Jones said the board was addressing the fallout and strengthening oversight, pointing to the creation of a committee to scrutinize the firm's security policies and export compliance. Nvidia has also retained the services of talent spotters Heidrick & Struggles to help find a new leader, according to Jones. Interim CEO and chief financial officer Colette Kress struck an upbeat tone on the company's Q3 earnings call. The results gave her plenty to work with : revenue rose 103 percent to $115.8 billion, while operating income climbed 115 percent to $77.5 billion. "We're addressing strong demand for compute across a diverse and expansive set of end customers, including hyperscalers, frontier labs, AI natives, enterprises, and governments," Kress said. She raised Nvidia's outlook for fiscal 2028, saying that the firm now expects revenue to grow approximately 75 percent year-on-year. Analysts immediately questioned this, asking what gave Kress the confidence to raise the outlook, given all the uncertainty surrounding the future direction of the company. Kress cited growing demand and additional supply as reasons for lifting the fiscal 2028 growth forecast from 70 to 75 percent. When asked about the financing deals that Nvidia provides for some of its customers, Kress appeared to hint that some things might change. "Our neoclouds have been so instrumental in terms of both supporting enterprises and supporting many of the different countries around the world, particularly on the sovereign perspective. And we continue to be working with them," she stated. But she added: "I think we would look at this and take a very strong look in terms of the types of companies that we would want to help in terms of the financing, as a lot of things have changed over this last quarter... but we do have some very, very strong existing customers that we will be continuing to work with." Kress also said that Nvidia's rack-scale Rubin platform had generated nearly $20 billion in revenue in its first quarter of production shipments. She said the firm expects the major frontier AI labs to account for approximately 15 percent of its Data Center revenue this year. Kress said that Nvidia is no longer shipping licensed products based on its Hopper silicon to China, as scrutiny grows over Beijing's access to advanced AI technology, and so its future guidance does not count on any Hopper revenue from there. Jones said the board was addressing the fallout and strengthening oversight, pointing to the creation of a committee to scrutinize the firm's security policies and export compliance. Nvidia has also retained the services of talent spotters Heidrick & Struggles to help find a new leader, according to Jones. Interim CEO and chief financial officer Colette Kress struck an upbeat tone on the company's Q3 earnings call. The results gave her plenty to work with : revenue rose 103 percent to $115.8 billion, while operating income climbed 115 percent to $77.5 billion. "We're addressing strong demand for compute across a diverse and expansive set of end customers, including hyperscalers, frontier labs, AI natives, enterprises, and governments," Kress said.
