Analysts immediately questioned this, asking what gave Kress the confidence to raise the outlook, given all the uncertainty surrounding the future direction of the company. Kress cited growing demand and additional supply as reasons for lifting the fiscal 2028 growth forecast from 70 to 75 percent. When asked about the financing deals that Nvidia provides for some of its customers, Kress appeared to hint that some things might change. "Our neoclouds have been so instrumental in terms of both supporting enterprises and supporting many of the different countries around the world, particularly on the sovereign perspective. And we continue to be working with them," she stated. But she added: "I think we would look at this and take a very strong look in terms of the types of companies that we would want to help in terms of the financing, as a lot of things have changed over this last quarter... but we do have some very, very strong existing customers that we will be continuing to work with." She said the firm expects the major frontier AI labs to account for approximately 15 percent of its Data Center revenue this year. Kress said that Nvidia is no longer shipping licensed products based on its Hopper silicon to China, as scrutiny grows over Beijing's access to advanced AI technology, and so its future guidance does not count on any Hopper revenue from there. Nvidia sold $2.4 billion worth of Hopper kit to China during Q3 after being given the go-ahead from the Trump administration to sell products like its H200 accelerators in China. Analysts say they expect doubts to remain over Nvidia's future despite the strong Q3 results as the quarter was already in the bag by the time the Huang scandal broke. "Nvidia's next battle is not against competitors alone. It must navigate export controls, sovereign AI initiatives, supply chain expansion, and rising capital intensity – all while protecting industry-leading margins," commented Forrester principal analyst Naveen Chhabra. "The market sees the biggest risk not in the financials, but the leadership and employee motivation amidst turmoil, which began only after the Q3 ended. The bigger risk is not near-term demand but operations, maintaining employee confidence, retaining talent, and preserving Nvidia's innovation culture." February's results should offer a clearer view of Nvidia after Huang. For now, the mighty AI platform biz expects another record quarter, forecasting revenue of $130 billion, give or take 3 percent. ®

item.title: Windows Server 2028 won't be compatible by default
item.description: Microsoft has pushed Windows Server 2028 into public preview, with an eye on beefed-up security, new infrastructure support, and the inevitable nod to AI. Neil Hinnant, a director on the Windows Server team, talked up the security tweaks. There's a hardened Server Core configuration by default and a new security baseline. "Trusted Launch extends protection to virtual machines," he wrote . "Confidential VM support begins a journey to support integrity-protected runtimes on supported CVM hardware." Server Core will therefore arrive locked down by default – good news for security, potentially less so for administrators whose existing configurations depend on more permissive settings. "For years, Windows Server shipped compatible by default," wrote Senior Product Manager Christina Curlette. "Making the server secure was up to you, usually by applying the Security Baseline or your own hardening scripts after setup." With Windows Server 2028 (and starting from Windows Server Insider Preview build 29706), Server Core will be installed hardened. "Hundreds of security settings are on from first boot," Curlette wrote. "Because the defaults are now locked down, some things that worked on Windows Server 2025 may not work on Windows Server 2028 without changes. This includes older protocols, legacy authentication, and some management tools and scripts." For a company obsessed with backward compatibility, this is quite the step. Welcome though the hardening is, administrators will need to test carefully: working on Windows Server 2025 won't guarantee a smooth ride in the brave new world. AI gets a role on both sides of the security fence: helping uncover vulnerabilities and giving Microsoft another reason to sell servers. Windows Server 2028 is being pitched for running models locally, with support for accelerators such as AMD's Instinct MI350P. Not every server is destined to babysit a model, however, and the storage changes may be more immediately useful to enterprise administrators. Windows Server 2028 will enable native NVMe storage by default, along with NVMe over TCP and RDMA. Booting from ReFS is also planned, adding another item to the storage upgrade list. Intune management for Windows Server has also entered preview. Azure Arc, with its cloud-native management workflows, is obviously still around, while Intune brings a more familiar management interface for administrators already using it for endpoints. Hinnant acknowledged that this was a "major release," and it looks like the security hardening alone will require a good deal of thought from administrators before organizations adopt the eventual production release. Esben Dochy, Principal Technical Evangelist for SecOps at Lansweeper, told The Register that Microsoft had indicated that the hardened security only applied to new installations. "Trusted Launch extends protection to virtual machines," he wrote . "Confidential VM support begins a journey to support integrity-protected runtimes on supported CVM hardware." Server Core will therefore arrive locked down by default – good news for security, potentially less so for administrators whose existing configurations depend on more permissive settings. "For years, Windows Server shipped compatible by default," wrote Senior Product Manager Christina Curlette. "Making the server secure was up to you, usually by applying the Security Baseline or your own hardening scripts after setup." With Windows Server 2028 (and starting from Windows Server Insider Preview build 29706), Server Core will be installed hardened. "Hundreds of security settings are on from first boot," Curlette wrote. "Because the defaults are now locked down, some things that worked on Windows Server 2025 may not work on Windows Server 2028 without changes. This includes older protocols, legacy authentication, and some management tools and scripts." For a company obsessed with backward compatibility, this is quite the step. Welcome though the hardening is, administrators will need to test carefully: working on Windows Server 2025 won't guarantee a smooth ride in the brave new world. AI gets a role on both sides of the security fence: helping uncover vulnerabilities and giving Microsoft another reason to sell servers. Windows Server 2028 is being pitched for running models locally, with support for accelerators such as AMD's Instinct MI350P. Not every server is destined to babysit a model, however, and the storage changes may be more immediately useful to enterprise administrators. Windows Server 2028 will enable native NVMe storage by default, along with NVMe over TCP and RDMA. Booting from ReFS is also planned, adding another item to the storage upgrade list. Intune management for Windows Server has also entered preview. Azure Arc, with its cloud-native management workflows, is obviously still around, while Intune brings a more familiar management interface for administrators already using it for endpoints. Hinnant acknowledged that this was a "major release," and it looks like the security hardening alone will require a good deal of thought from administrators before organizations adopt the eventual production release. Esben Dochy, Principal Technical Evangelist for SecOps at Lansweeper, told The Register that Microsoft had indicated that the hardened security only applied to new installations. "If that remains in the final release," he said, "in-place upgrades could be easier. The catch is that those servers may also miss out on the new security defaults." "Hardening is the right direction," he said, "but it will add work for teams moving to Server 2028." According to Lansweeper’s figures, as of October 2026, Windows Server 2019 ruled the roost with 33 percent. Windows Server 2025 had reached just 7 percent. "From behavior we've seen in the past," said Dochy, "adoption is primarily driven by lifecycle, so until the more used versions start going EOL, I don't expect much adoption, similar to what Server 2025 is experiencing." Windows Server 2025 remains under extended support until 2034, but Microsoft's direction of travel is clear: beefed-up security by default, a home for AI applications, and Intune management for fleets of servers. ®

item.title: India's SatLeo Labs wants to build a 'thermometer for Earth' in space
item.description:
Sharmila Kuthunur is an independent space journalist based in Bengaluru, India. Her work has also appeared in Scientific American, Science, Astronomy and Live Science, among other publications. She holds a master's degree in journalism from Northeastern University in Boston. 

AHMEDABAD, India — As climate disasters grow more frequent and severe, a young Indian space-tech startup is betting it can help the world act sooner by reading Earth's temperature from orbit in near-real time. SatLeo Labs, based here in western India, is building what it calls a " thermometer for Earth " in space. It plans to achieve its roadmap to deliver frequent, near-real-time thermal data through Pyro, a planned constellation of 15 microsatellites that will circle the planet in low Earth orbit by early 2030, if all goes to plan. Equipped with thermal sensors and onboard artificial intelligence , the satellites will measure the heat radiating from Earth's surface at a resolution finer than 10 meters (33 feet), which is sharp enough to map heat variations down to street level, the company says. "It's going to be that precise," SatLeo Labs co-founder Urmil Bakhai told Space.com in a recent interview. That level of detail, he said, helps distinguish temperatures across a single city and pinpoint urban hot spots, allowing governments and policymakers to plan targeted interventions and more heat-resilient city designs. The company is also targeting agriculture, and for good reason: Research suggests that thermal data can directly reveal water stress on crops days before leaves wilt, discolor or show other visible damage, unlike visible-light satellite imagery. Other uses the company is eyeing include spotting forest fires early, tracking industrial emissions and, on the defense side, detecting sudden temperature spikes from missile launches . Down the road, the team also envisions hyper-local uses. Near the top of its list are live heat maps built into navigation apps that could help gig-economy workers in India. These folks, who often ride motorcycles, could use the data to pick cooler routes during heat waves, said Bakhai. "We are in space, but we're solving problems on Earth ," said Shravan Bhati, SatLeo's co-founder and CEO. First, however, the company has to prove that its homegrown hardware works in space. On Oct. 1, SatLeo launched its first technology demonstrator, TAPAS-1, aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket as part of the Transporter-18 rideshare mission. Short for "Thermal Access Platform for Analytics & Solutions," TAPAS-1 is India's first commercial thermal payload in orbit and the first of SatLeo's three planned test payloads meant to validate its technology. Once complete, the 15-satellite Pyro fleet will scan all of the world's land surface at least twice a day, Bakhai said. Successful deployment of that fleet would make SatLeo one of just a few private thermal-imaging operators across the world, such as SatVu in the U.K. and OroraTech in Germany. The

item.content:encoded:
Sharmila Kuthunur is an independent space journalist based in Bengaluru, India. Her work has also appeared in Scientific American, Science, Astronomy and Live Science, among other publications. She holds a master's degree in journalism from Northeastern University in Boston. 

AHMEDABAD, India — As climate disasters grow more frequent and severe, a young Indian space-tech startup is betting it can help the world act sooner by reading Earth's temperature from orbit in near-real time. SatLeo Labs, based here in western India, is building what it calls a " thermometer for Earth " in space. It plans to achieve its roadmap to deliver frequent, near-real-time thermal data through Pyro, a planned constellation of 15 microsatellites that will circle the planet in low Earth orbit by early 2030, if all goes to plan. Equipped with thermal sensors and onboard artificial intelligence , the satellites will measure the heat radiating from Earth's surface at a resolution finer than 10 meters (33 feet), which is sharp enough to map heat variations down to street level, the company says. "It's going to be that precise," SatLeo Labs co-founder Urmil Bakhai told Space.com in a recent interview. That level of detail, he said, helps distinguish temperatures across a single city and pinpoint urban hot spots, allowing governments and policymakers to plan targeted interventions and more heat-resilient city designs. The company is also targeting agriculture, and for good reason: Research suggests that thermal data can directly reveal water stress on crops days before leaves wilt, discolor or show other visible damage, unlike visible-light satellite imagery. Other uses the company is eyeing include spotting forest fires early, tracking industrial emissions and, on the defense side, detecting sudden temperature spikes from missile launches . Down the road, the team also envisions hyper-local uses. Near the top of its list are live heat maps built into navigation apps that could help gig-economy workers in India. These folks, who often ride motorcycles, could use the data to pick cooler routes during heat waves, said Bakhai. "We are in space, but we're solving problems on Earth ," said Shravan Bhati, SatLeo's co-founder and CEO. First, however, the company has to prove that its homegrown hardware works in space. On Oct. 1, SatLeo launched its first technology demonstrator, TAPAS-1, aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket as part of the Transporter-18 rideshare mission. Short for "Thermal Access Platform for Analytics & Solutions," TAPAS-1 is India's first commercial thermal payload in orbit and the first of SatLeo's three planned test payloads meant to validate its technology. Once complete, the 15-satellite Pyro fleet will scan all of the world's land surface at least twice a day, Bakhai said. Successful deployment of that fleet would make SatLeo one of just a few private thermal-imaging operators across the world, such as SatVu in the U.K. and OroraTech in Germany. The company has raised roughly $6 million since it was founded in 2023, and it holds letters of intent worth $54 million from prospective customers, Bakhai said. An illustration of SatLeo Labs' temperature-mapping payload. (Image credit: SatLeo Labs) 'Space is the only solution' SatLeo grew out of a government project that used satellite data for farming insights. Its founders found existing thermal data, such as from the U.S. government's Landsat satellites or Earth-observing craft operated by the San Francisco company Planet Labs , too coarse for India's fragmented farmlands, Bakhai said. When field teams and drones couldn't fill the gap at scale, "we realized space is the only solution," he said. SatLeo's orbital ambitions take shape on the ground, inside a light-blocked cleanroom at the company's headquarters here in Ahmedabad. When Space.com visited in late October, about three weeks after TAPAS-1 launched, a handful of engineers in cleanroom coats were already fine-tuning its successor, TAPAS-2. The payload itself sat perched on a solitary, nondescript table with a thick, hole-filled steel top meant to dampen vibrations from footsteps, traffic and the like. The room's only window was covered by a thick black blind to seal out stray light, a necessity for calibrating sensors meant to track the planet's thermal pulse from a few hundred kilometers up. Despite its small size, the payload is built to collect enormous amounts of data. How much detail a payload can capture "all depends upon the architecture of the detector," said SatLeo co-founder Ranendu Ghosh, a former scientist at the Indian Space Research Organisation ( ISRO ). The design captures two infrared bands, mid-wave and long-wave, on the same payload. The company says this lets a single design serve both civilian and defense uses: long-wave suits applications like agriculture, while the hotter signatures of fires or missile launches show up better in mid-wave. SatLeo Labs tests the payload for its TAPAS-1 satellite mission, which launched on Oct. 1, 2026. (Image credit: SatLeo Labs) 'Zeal to deliver in time' TAPAS-1 took just six months to build, and TAPAS-2 is on a similar timeline: It's expected to be ready by February 2027, according to the team. Access to government test facilities explains much of that speed, Bhati said. Rather than buy capital-intensive equipment, such as a thermal vacuum chamber that mimics conditions in space, the company calibrates its payloads at facilities run by IN-SPACe, the government agency that supports private space firms, and ISRO's Space Applications Centre, both in Ahmedabad. A small group of former ISRO scientists, about eight among a staff of around 40, also mentored the younger workforce and "really made this journey a little faster for us," Bakhai said. Ghosh, who spent more than two decades at ISRO, said the nature of a private company helps, too. "When I was in ISRO, I saw people delivering this kind of a payload," he said. "I never saw it delivered in less than a year." He credited the SatLeo team's "zeal to deliver in time," along with fewer administrative challenges than at ISRO, which he described as an organization where "you cannot bypass the hierarchy." The harder constraint, the founders said, is not building satellites but finding rockets to carry them to space. TAPAS-1's launch slipped from a planned February liftoff to October for lack of a ride, Bakhai said. SpaceX is reportedly not accepting new bookings until at least 2029. In addition, Skyroot Aerospace, which in July became the first Indian company to reach orbit , is still flying development missions meant to validate its Vikram-1 rocket before it begins full-scale commercial operations. SatLeo Labs' TAPAS-1 satellite (to left of arrow) deploys from the upper stage of a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket on the Transporter-18 rideshare mission on Oct. 1, 2026. (Image credit: SatLeo Labs/SpaceX) "There is a challenge right now in terms of availability of launch vehicles," Bakhai said. Once additional Indian rockets, such as those built by Skyroot and Agnikul , are flying regularly, "things will be much easier." SatLeo is among more than 400 space startups that have emerged in India since the government opened the sector to private participation in 2020. Driven by this new wave of private enterprise, the country's space economy — currently valued at about $9 billion — is estimated to reach $40 billion over the next decade. Asked what advice they would give newcomers entering the growing industry, SatLeo's three co-founders offered a unified message for success: start with the problem, then decide what to build. "If you're solving a problem," Bhati said, "then people will bet on you."

item.title: Police arrest 15 over £1.5M 'we'll recover your losses' scam targeting elderly
item.description: Fifteen people have been arrested over an alleged scam that squeezed more money from investment fraud victims by offering to help recover their losses. City of London Police searched 17 London addresses on November 11 and apprehended 14 men and one woman. All have since been released on bail. Investigators say the suspected fraudsters posed as regulators to persuade previous victims that compensation was available. Reports submitted through the UK's Report Fraud service helped investigators trace the compensation pitch to around 3,000 recipients since October 2025. Most victims were elderly, police said. The offers arrived by letter and email, promising redress for earlier investment losses. City of London Police said the victims were initially targeted by a range of investment scams related to art, carbon credits, land, whisky, wine, and pensions, and that some took place more than a decade prior to their re-victimization. Targets were directed to a company that demanded a holding fee before supposedly reclaiming their money. Police say those who paid were left further out of pocket. "Today's action sends a clear message to those who target vulnerable people for financial gain: you will be pursued and will face robust action," said Nik Adams, deputy commissioner at the City of London Police. "Behind every fraud report is a real person whose trust has been damaged, and in some cases, whose life savings have been stolen. We know the impact of these crimes can be devastating. "This case highlights the importance of reporting fraud through the Report Fraud service. Information provided by victims helped investigators link reports together, uncover the wider conspiracy, and identify those involved. It is a powerful reminder that every report counts and can play a vital role in bringing offenders to justice." The investigation also extends beyond London, with police identifying locations linked to the case in Kent and Hertfordshire. The searches resulted in officers seizing cash, drugs, and other high-value items, including a watch worth around £230,000, with the total haul valued at more than £2 million. Police put losses identified so far at £1.5 million and expect that figure to rise as the investigation continues. Knowing the details of an earlier scam doesn't make a caller trustworthy, police warned. That information can be used to sell victims a second fraud. Report Fraud has also highlighted substantial losses in other scams affecting older people. Fraudsters exploiting positions of trust stole a reported £93.8 million during 2025/26. People aged 70 and over lost more than £51 million, with relatives, friends, carers, and others entrusted with their finances among the perpetrators. Report Fraud received 3,812 reports in this category. "The impact of fraud extends far beyond financial loss, especially when it is carried out by those who are trusted by the victim," said Mark Evans, president at the Law Society of England and Wales. item.title: Voyager 1 at one light-day: Historian revisits Golden Record's forgotten details
item.description: In the one light-day that humanity's most distant object has now traveled from Earth, there has been enough time for details about its creation—and what it left behind—to be discovered again. Voyager 1, which left Earth in 1977 on an initial mission to fly by Jupiter and Saturn (as well as the latter's moon Titan), crossed into interstellar space in 2012. Like its twin (Voyager 2), Voyager 1 carries a "commemorative phonograph record," in part as a nod to the 100th anniversary of the recording medium and as a message from humanity to whoever (or whatever) encounters the spacecraft on its journey through outer space. About those forgotten bits, ask Glen Swanson . While researching the history of the Golden Record, he uncovered the discs' overlooked second set of operating directions and located the duplicates that were made and distributed almost five decades ago. Read full article Comments

item.title: Netflix, Fox and the $2bn bid for the 2030 World Cup that could reshape live sports
item.description: The battle for the US TV rights to the tournament will pit the traditional broadcaster against the ‘whatever-it-takes’ streamer. It could be a tipping point in the industry The awarding of broadcast rights in the United States for this year’s World Cup was a cut-price deal to avoid legal action from the existing rights holders, Fox Sports. This week’s tender process for the 2030 tournament will be anything but. Media rights and broadcast experts canvassed by the Guardian in the US and Europe are united in agreement that Fifa will benefit from the most competitive and expensive auction in the competition’s history. It is expected to fetch between $1.5bn (£1.13bn) and $2bn, with some predicting the outcome could be a landmark moment for the sports and entertainment industry. Continue reading...

item.title: ‘When I walked for Burberry I met Kanye West’: the two lives of Bromley footballer Omar Sowunmi
item.description: Full-time defender and part-time model, the 31-year-old is happy to shine a light on both sides of his dual career “I was walking down the street one day and someone came up to me and said: ‘I think you should be a model,’” the Bromley defender Omar Sowunmi says. He was already living out many people’s dreams as a professional footballer but was able to assume an alter ego in the world of fashion. There are few parallels between the grind of lower-league football and Milan fashion week but the 31-year-old is adept in both worlds. Sowunmi’s dual career mixes trips to Doncaster with visits to Paris. On Saturday Bromley travel to Reading under their new manager, Karl Robinson, as they attempt to move off the bottom of League One and the centre-back is clear where his focus lies even after his chance encounter with a model agency employee expanded his horizons. Continue reading...

item.title: Annoying Trump and dodging Flock: inside MapQuest’s contrarian comeback
item.description: After refusing to obey the president’s Lake Ontario order, MapQuest briefly rose to No 1 in navigation apps. It’s now a tool in the US anti-surveillance movement I am among the legion of former PC desk occupants with warm memories of MapQuest, the Y2K-era travel website that kept millennial drivers on course with sheaves of printed-out directions – a quantum leap over the ungainly glovebox map. But I assumed it had long since gone the way of AIM and Skype, its manual turn-by-turn guidance made obsolete by big tech. Proof of life came in January 2025, when Donald Trump issued an executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America – a change Apple Maps and Google Maps promptly adopted, while MapQuest … did nothing. Not only had it never signed off, MapQuest was reinventing itself as a plucky oppositional hero, the app most likely to uphold your geographical beliefs. Continue reading...

item.title: ULA says Vulcan lacked the oomph to get Amazon satellites to orbit
item.description: United Launch Alliance (ULA) says poor booster performance appears to have doomed Sunday's Vulcan mission, which lost an Amazon Leo satellite payload on the rocket's return to flight. ULA's initial assessment points to trouble almost immediately. "Early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance," it said. As a result, stage separation occurred at too low an altitude, and the rocket was not traveling fast enough for the payload to reach orbit. The second stage appeared to perform well, with its RL10 engines operating as planned, but that wasn't enough to make up for the shortfall, and the mission failed . ULA lost telemetry approximately ten minutes into flight. An investigation is underway, led by ULA and overseen by the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), which had to activate two Debris Response Areas where debris was falling. The agency directs aircraft to leave these areas, and others are prevented from entering. Late Wednesday afternoon GMT, ULA posted an update stating that it looks like it might be the fuel supply rather than the BE-4 engines that caused the underperformance of the booster. The company wrote: “Preliminary indications are that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines." Previous flights had been blighted by problems with the solid rocket boosters , designed to give the rocket a kick at launch. Those issues prompted a stand-down while investigators examined the cause. This time, ULA said: "All indications are that the solid rocket booster performance was nominal, following nozzle improvements implemented for this launch." Attention therefore turns to Vulcan's liquid-fueled core stage, powered by two Blue Origin BE-4 engines, though that does not establish an engine fault. Fuel delivery or another first-stage system could also be responsible, and the investigation is ongoing. The BE-4 also powers Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, which exploded on the launchpad during a ground test in May. In August, Blue Origin boss Dave Limp said that the issue originated at the main oxygen valve on one of the BE-4 engines. Modifications were made to deal with the problem. The upper stage's apparently normal performance may offer some reassurance to NASA, although the investigation remains at an early stage. The agency dropped the delayed Exploration Upper Stage earlier this year and is pursuing a stretched Centaur V alongside its existing interim cryogenic propulsion stage as options for Artemis IV. NASA is targeting Artemis IV for early 2028 and Artemis V for later that year. ULA said: "We truly understand the impact this has on our customers and are committed to returning to flight as safely and quickly as we can." The failure also dents ULA's otherwise impressive launch record. A predecessor of Vulcan, the Atlas V, has a 100 percent success record for payloads reaching orbit. Howeve

item.title: 1 light-day from Earth! NASA's Voyager 1 probe hits huge milestone in interstellar space
item.description: null NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is now one light-day from Earth — so far away that it takes signals a full 24 hours to reach the probe. Voyager 1 launched on Sept. 5, 1977, just a couple of weeks after Voyager 2 lifted off. But Voyager 1 launched on a faster trajectory than its twin and has just become the first spacecraft to ever reach one light-day away, which is equivalent to about 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers), or the distance that one light particle travels in 24 hours. The milestone — which Voyager 1 hit today (Nov. 18) at 5:16 a.m. EST (1016 GMT) — shows the incredible ingenuity, technical ability and creativity from the teams at NASA that continue to innovate to keep this mission going nearly five decades later. "The Earth and Voyager are exactly 24 hours apart at the speed of light," Voyager Project Scientist Linda Spilker told Space.com. "It's a very special moment where Voyager 1 is about 16.1 billion miles away, and we're celebrating that moment because it's the first human-made object to actually reach one light-day distance." All things Voyager The two Voyager spacecraft have been on one serious ride since launching in 1977. And each of these twin probes has taken a unique and historic journey through our solar system and beyond. On Voyager 1's trip through our cosmic neighborhood, for example, it made countless groundbreaking observations of planets and moons that we had never before seen up close (or at all). The probe discovered a ring around Jupiter as well as the planet's moons Thebe and Metis. It also found five new moons and a new ring around Saturn. "Voyager 1 flew past the Jupiter system and took images of Jupiter's moon Io, and it actually discovered that Io is volcanically active. So, images that were taken showed these volcanoes that were actively erupting, and we learned that Io is actually the most volcanically active body in our solar system, which is just amazing," Cynthia Phillips, a project scientist for NASA's Europa Clipper mission, told Space.com about one of Voyager 1's many discoveries. item.content:encoded: null NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is now one light-day from Earth — so far away that it takes signals a full 24 hours to reach the probe. Voyager 1 launched on Sept. 5, 1977, just a couple of weeks after Voyager 2 lifted off. But Voyager 1 launched on a faster trajectory than its twin and has just become the first spacecraft to ever reach one light-day away, which is equivalent to about 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers), or the distance that one light particle travels in 24 hours. The milestone — which Voyager 1 hit today (Nov. 18) at 5:16 a.m. EST (1016 GMT) — shows the incredible ingenuity, technical ability and creativity from the teams at NASA that continue to innovate to keep this mission going nearly five decades later. "The Earth and Voyager are exactly 24 hours apart at the speed of light," Voyager Project Scientist Linda Spilker told Space.com. "It's a very special moment where Voyager 1 is about 16.1 billion miles away, and we're celebrating that moment because it's the first human-made object to actually reach one light-day distance." All things Voyager The two Voyager spacecraft have been on one serious ride since launching in 1977. And each of these twin probes has taken a unique and historic journey through our solar system and beyond. On Voyager 1's trip through our cosmic neighborhood, for example, it made countless groundbreaking observations of planets and moons that we had never before seen up close (or at all). The probe discovered a ring around Jupiter as well as the planet's moons Thebe and Metis. It also found five new moons and a new ring around Saturn. "Voyager 1 flew past the Jupiter system and took images of Jupiter's moon Io, and it actually discovered that Io is volcanically active. So, images that were taken showed these volcanoes that were actively erupting, and we learned that Io is actually the most volcanically active body in our solar system, which is just amazing," Cynthia Phillips, a project scientist for NASA's Europa Clipper mission, told Space.com about one of Voyager 1's many discoveries. The Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 probes both flew past Jupiter in 1979, on their way out of the solar system. Represented here is Voyager 2's encounter with Jupiter. NASA/JPL A close-up of Jupiter's Great Red Spot as seen by one of NASA's Voyager spacecraft. NASA/JPL-Caltech Voyager 1 took photos of Jupiter and two of its satellites (Io, left, and Europa). The new study says that moons orbiting a gas giant planet greater than 8 Jupiter masses could help astronomers detect a rogue planet. NASA/JPL A mosaic of Jupiter by Voyager 1. JPL Jupiter and two of its moons — Io, to the left, and Europa — as seen by Voyager 1 on Feb. 13, 1979. JPL/NASA Voyager 1 image of Jupiter's volcanic moon Io, showing the active plume of a volcano called Loki. NASA/JPL/USGS "And then, as Voyager 1 continued out to the Saturn system, it actually discovered that Saturn's large moon Titan has a very thick atmosphere surrounding it," she added. "So it's one of the only moons that has a thick atmosphere." Decades later, Voyager 1's data is still incredibly important for scientists studying the planets and moons of our cosmic neighborhood. Phillips works on Clipper, which is on its way to study Jupiter's ocean moon Europa. And the basis of that work stems from early observations by Voyager. "Every time I get to use data from Voyager, I have to kind of think back to where that data came from," Phillips said. "I think about kind of the legacy, the missions that really set the precedent for a mission like Europa Clipper. Voyager is right there at the top of the list. And some of those images that we took with the Voyager 1 and 2 spacecraft of Europa — they're actually still, for some portions of Europa, they're the best pictures that we have. So, we're still using that data today, almost 50 years later." Today, Voyager 1 and 2 are both exploring interstellar space. On Aug. 25, 2012, Voyager 1 became the first human-made object to leave the heliosphere, or the protective bubble of solar particles that surrounds the planets and other objects in our solar system. After crossing that boundary, Voyager 1 entered interstellar space and has been exploring the interstellar medium ever since. Voyager 2 followed suit in November 2018. While the Voyager spacecraft have left the heliosphere, they have technically not left the solar system, as they are still within the gravitational influence of the sun. Today, Voyager 1 is traveling 38,000 mph (61,155 kph) through interstellar space, exploring farther than any human-made object in history. You need patience The Voyager mission team communicates with Voyager in radio waves via the Deep Space Network, a collective of giant radio antennas that NASA uses to "talk" to a wide range of far-off spacecraft. And since radio waves travel at the speed of light, it now takes 24 hours for communications to reach Voyager 1, and then another 24 hours for any response to return. The Canberra Complex of the Deep Space Network located in Australia. (Image credit: NASA) "You need to have patience because now, if you send a command to Voyager, Voyager receives that command 24 hours later," Spilker said. "So two days later, you receive confirmation that yes, Voyager one received your command and is sending back the information that you'd like it to send back." That patience is important, as the nearly-50-year-old Voyager mission is still actively making science observations and collecting new data. While some of the probes' science instruments have had to be shut off over the years to save battery life, both probes are still going strong. "It is always difficult when an instrument has to get turned off, knowing that it has returned good science data for so many years," Spilker said. "But a plan was laid down to make sure we had at least one instrument operating on each spacecraft, one type of instrument, for as long as we could." As long as the mission is active, the team will continue to investigate the unknown with Voyager. After all, ever since the probes entered interstellar space, they have been exploring areas of space that we've only ever studied remotely or in theory. An illustration showing how NASA's Hubble Space Telescope looks along the paths of NASA's Voyager 1 and 2 spacecraft as they have traveled through the solar system and into interstellar space. (Image credit: NASA, ESA, and Z. Levay (STScI)) "Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause in 2012, and what we knew about interstellar space at that point really came just from remote observations and theories. And so, right away, Voyager started to find that what we expected was not exactly right," Spilker said. So far, the team has found that the sun's influence extends much farther from the heliopause than they expected. The Voyagers have observed and measured "ripples coming from the sun," as Spilker described them, deep in interstellar space. "Voyager is going to continue to measure the cosmic rays and particles, and also the radio waves coming from interstellar space and coming from the sun," Spilker said, adding that the team is always eagerly "waiting to see if there might be more surprises out there." An enduring legacy How has this mission from the 1970s continued to not just survive but actively push forward through all of that time, overcoming countless hurdles and unexpected challenges? "Voyager's longevity is really a tribute to all of the people who worked on Voyager, from those who designed the spacecraft, built it, programmed its computers, launched it, and then the teams of individuals that have flown it over that 50 years," Spilker said. item.title: Beyoncé Becomes First Artist in Grammy History to Earn 100 Nominations!
item.description: Beyoncé becomes the first artist in history to reach 100 career Grammy nominations. Photo Credit: Beyoncé/Instagram If you have ever wondered what triple digits look like on music’s biggest stage, Beyoncé just gave everyone the answer. The Houston-born global music superstar has officially become the first artist in history to reach 100 career Grammy nominations, hitting the milestone with her latest nod for “ Morning Dew ( Donk )”, which is nominated for Best R&B Solo Performance at the 69th Annual Grammy Awards (2027 Grammys). Released in July 2026 ahead of the 20th anniversary of her sophomore album B’Day, “Morning Dew (Donk)” puts her in a category alongside Kehlani , Victoria Monét , Jill Scott , and Nigerian star Tems . To put the 100-nomination milestone into perspective, no other recording artist has ever crossed into triple digits since the Grammys began. Beyoncé had previously been tied with her husband, Jay-Z , at 88 nominations each before breaking that tie in 2024 with 11 nods for Cowboy Carter to reach 99—and this latest recognition pushes her even further ahead as the artist with the highest number of Grammy nominations in history. Beyoncé holding her three Grammy trophies at the 67th Annual Grammy Awards in 2025. Photo Credit: Beyoncé/Instagram It is also a good reminder of how long she has been doing this at the highest level. Beyoncé’s Grammy journey started all the way back in 2000 as part of Destiny’s Child with “Bills, Bills, Bills”, and across more than two decades as a solo artist, group member, and collaborator, she has built a record that keeps stretching further ahead of the pack. Alongside holding the title for the most Grammy nominations of all time, she is already the most awarded artist in Grammy history with 35 wins, a record she first broke in 2023 when she surpassed late conductor Georg Solti ’s 31 trophies. She pushed that tally even higher at the 2025 Grammys, taking home three awards—Album of the Year and Best Country Album for Cowboy Carter, as well as Best Country Duo/Group Performance for “II Most Wanted” alongside Miley Cyrus . Now all eyes turn to Sunday, 7 February 2027, when the 2027 Grammy Awards take place at the Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles and we find out whether nomination number 100 turns into Grammy win number 36. The post Beyoncé Becomes First Artist in Grammy History to Earn 100 Nominations! appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: UK.gov JV gets £178M Home Office hosting deal. Without competition
item.description: The Home Office has awarded a contract worth £178 million to a public-private hosting services joint venture - without competition - to support critical national infrastructure. According to a notice published last week , Crown Hosting Data Centres (CHDC) won the seven-year contract to support "essential national infrastructure underpinning the Home Office's most critical systems, including border security, the Police National Computer (PNC), and core intelligence environments." CHDC is a joint venture between the Cabinet Office, which owns 25 percent, and Ark Data Centres Ltd, which owns the rest. It was set up in 2015 for the express purpose of providing hosting services for the government. The award was made through an existing framework agreement, set up in February 2022, awarded to CHDC without competition via a Voluntary Ex-Ante Transparency Notice . The service is set to support Critical National Infrastructure, although the notice does not reveal specific services requested. Mention of continued support for the Police National Computer may raise eyebrows. The Home Office is managing the transition of the aging legacy system to the Law Enforcement Data Service (LEDS) under the National Law Enforcement Data Program (NLEDP). A notice in December 2024 said that the Home Office was "focused on the development and adoption of LEDS products to replace existing PNC capability across all police forces and other non-policing PNC consumers, enabling the retirement by March 2026 (the point at which PNC support will expire)." The government had previously set a target of decommissioning the PNC in 2022. The Register has asked the Home Office to clarify why Crown Hosting support is necessary beyond this date. The PNC – which is based on mainframe technology dating from the 1970s – was at the center of a scandal in 2021 when a technology failure led to the loss of 413,000 records of evidence . The incident, which left then Prime Minister Boris Johnson floundering in Parliament, was the result of a scripting error in code designed to weed out records to be deleted from the PNC, a system running on a Fujitsu BS2000/OSD SE700-30 mainframe-based at a datacenter in Hendon, London. In 2022, the Cabinet Office awarded a contract worth up to £250 million to CHDC, also without outside competition. ®

item.title: Grand Theft Auto VI: The Ars Technica review
item.description: Just a minute ago, I was shooting my way out of a cocaine deal gone wrong, darting behind furniture for cover. Now I’m sitting on the floor of my home, working through the instructions to construct an Ikea-style coffee table with my partner. A tiny heart with a plus sign pops up, showing that our relationship is stronger for this quotidian domestic effort. This is the contrast at the heart of Grand Theft Auto VI , a game that seems to revel in both action movie bombast and the mundanities of everyday life for an up-and-coming young criminal couple. The reimagined and expanded Vice City is still the grand, crude, satirical criminal playground you’d expect after 25 years of 3D Grand Theft Auto games. And that world is as full, detailed, technically impressive, and polished as you would expect after this latest installment received a reported billion-dollar budget and roughly a decade of development work involving thousands of Rockstar staffers. Read full article Comments

item.title: SAP opens AI to on-prem customers, but cloud commitments could shut smaller firms out
item.description: SAP's commercial terms could put its latest AI tools out of reach for many customers, particularly smaller businesses running a single ERP system, the new chair of its German-speaking user group has warned. Thomas Henzler, appointed chair of DSAG last month, told The Register that Joule Studio 2.0 – SAP's upgraded platform for developing and deploying AI agents to automate business tasks – is a leap forward. Yet DSAG, which represents SAP users in Germany, Switzerland, and Austria, remains in talks with the vendor about the commercial conditions attached to access. In July 2023, CEO Christian Klein told investors that SAP's "newest innovations and capabilities" will only be delivered in the public or private cloud using RISE with SAP, the vendor's lift-shift-and-transform program launched with partners and cloud providers in early 2021. Customers running ERP software on-premises, or hosting it with a hyperscaler outside RISE, will miss out, he said. However, in May this year, SAP appeared to perform a U-turn . It said on-premises customers could access Joule 2.0 if they commit to a cloud "journey" through RISE with SAP, changing their support and commercial arrangements while migration projects are still underway. Henzler told The Reg : "There is a gap between the customer's reality and SAP's strategy for the autonomous enterprise. A lot of customers are still planning to migrate to S/4HANA, and now the question is, 'what do we have to do to use SAP AI, and what does it mean regarding the cloud strategy?' "Now it's a completely new strategy, a new approach, and a new underlying technology. The question is, what does it mean for existing projects, S/4HANA migrations, cloud migrations and so on? Is it necessary to rethink all the projects? Is there a big shift in the technology and architectures?" The DSAG chair said the biggest challenge in connecting legacy on-prem systems, such as ECC, to the new Joule suite is the commercial model. "Access requires a substantial RISE commitment and a minimum cloud-to-on-premise maintenance ratio. In practice, this creates a problem for customers with only one ECC system. To meet the cloud threshold, they have to convert their entire on-premises maintenance into a cloud subscription, which defeats the purpose of an on-premises connector. Consequently, the model only works for large enterprises with multiple SAP ERP systems that can, for example, migrate one system after the other to unlock AI for the rest," he said. "In the end, to get the benefit you have to start a RISE with SAP migration. Therefore, the connector doesn't make sense for the majority of SME customers. From my perspective, this approach works only for large customers with multiple ERP systems, for example, if they take one system, move it to the cloud, and then another one. Then they can use AI, because they reach the needed ratio to use the on-prem connector. That is more or less a commercial approach. We need a solution for all customers, inde

item.content:encoded: SAP's commercial terms could put its latest AI tools out of reach for many customers, particularly smaller businesses running a single ERP system, the new chair of its German-speaking user group has warned. Thomas Henzler, appointed chair of DSAG last month, told The Register that Joule Studio 2.0 – SAP's upgraded platform for developing and deploying AI agents to automate business tasks – is a leap forward. Yet DSAG, which represents SAP users in Germany, Switzerland, and Austria, remains in talks with the vendor about the commercial conditions attached to access. In July 2023, CEO Christian Klein told investors that SAP's "newest innovations and capabilities" will only be delivered in the public or private cloud using RISE with SAP, the vendor's lift-shift-and-transform program launched with partners and cloud providers in early 2021. Customers running ERP software on-premises, or hosting it with a hyperscaler outside RISE, will miss out, he said. However, in May this year, SAP appeared to perform a U-turn . It said on-premises customers could access Joule 2.0 if they commit to a cloud "journey" through RISE with SAP, changing their support and commercial arrangements while migration projects are still underway. Henzler told The Reg : "There is a gap between the customer's reality and SAP's strategy for the autonomous enterprise. A lot of customers are still planning to migrate to S/4HANA, and now the question is, 'what do we have to do to use SAP AI, and what does it mean regarding the cloud strategy?' "Now it's a completely new strategy, a new approach, and a new underlying technology. The question is, what does it mean for existing projects, S/4HANA migrations, cloud migrations and so on? Is it necessary to rethink all the projects? Is there a big shift in the technology and architectures?" The DSAG chair said the biggest challenge in connecting legacy on-prem systems, such as ECC, to the new Joule suite is the commercial model. "Access requires a substantial RISE commitment and a minimum cloud-to-on-premise maintenance ratio. In practice, this creates a problem for customers with only one ECC system. To meet the cloud threshold, they have to convert their entire on-premises maintenance into a cloud subscription, which defeats the purpose of an on-premises connector. Consequently, the model only works for large enterprises with multiple SAP ERP systems that can, for example, migrate one system after the other to unlock AI for the rest," he said. "In the end, to get the benefit you have to start a RISE with SAP migration. Therefore, the connector doesn't make sense for the majority of SME customers. From my perspective, this approach works only for large customers with multiple ERP systems, for example, if they take one system, move it to the cloud, and then another one. Then they can use AI, because they reach the needed ratio to use the on-prem connector. That is more or less a commercial approach. We need a solution for all customers, independent of the commercials." The Register asked SAP to respond to Henzler's concerns. A spokesperson said: "The offering separates a customer's commercial commitment to cloud ERP from the timing of its operational migration. Customers that meet the applicable commercial and technical requirements can use supported AI capabilities with eligible ECC or on-premises SAP S/4HANA systems while modernizing their landscape. Eligibility is not determined by the number of ERP instances and can therefore also extend to single-instance customers." There are thousands of SAP ERP users worldwide, including some of the world's largest businesses. Despite efforts to get them onto the latest iteration – S/4HANA – and in the cloud, where the vendor promised it could gather a greater "share of wallet" from customers , there has been a dogged resistance to these complex and time-consuming migrations. Gartner figures for Q4 2024 showed only 39 percent of worldwide ECC customers – from a total of 35,000 – had bought or subscribed to SAP S/4HANA licenses. More recently, The Reg uncovered that SAP was about €2 billion short of its target for getting customers off on-prem support. Customers still running older ERP systems face pressure to embrace AI-supported automation. Whether SAP's terms help them do that – or simply help move them onto RISE – remains the question. ®

item.title: ‘My family would kill me if they saw it’: the ‘harmless’ images that can be deadly for women in Pakistan
item.description: Tech companies urged to adapt moderation of photos online that can trigger violence against women in some countries It was just a photo of a smiling girl in jeans and a vest top, the kind of outfit any young woman might wear in any country. But for Maniza*, a teenager from a conservative town in Pakistan who never leaves the house without her hijab, the selfie she took at home put her at very real risk of an “honour” killing. “My family are really strict and I always wore a hijab. My father didn’t want me to stay in school but my mum pushed him. He said if I got into trouble, he would kill me. It wasn’t just words, he meant it,” she says. Continue reading...

item.title: From Bronze-Brown Traditional Attire to Bridal Lace, See Tomi Thomas & Efya’s Wedding Looks
item.description: Newlyweds Efya and Tomi Thomas at their white wedding reception in Accra. Photo Credit: Thret Studio/Instagram Two music stars, two countries, one beautiful love story! Nigerian singer Tomi Thomas and Ghanaian songstress Efya have made things official, celebrating their union in Accra with a wedding that brought Nigerian and Ghanaian traditions together. From their coordinated traditional looks to their elegant white wedding outfits and a song Tomi made especially for his bride, there was plenty to love about this celebration. If you’ve followed the music scenes in Nigeria and Ghana, you’ll know that Tomi and Efya have each carved out their own place in contemporary African music. Tomi Thomas, who hails from Delta State, Nigeria, first gained recognition as part of the music collective L.O.S (Loud On Sound), before building a solo catalogue that moves across Afro-fusion and alternative sounds. Efya, born Jane Awindor in Kumasi, Ghana, is one of the country’s most celebrated vocalists, known for her soulful music and multiple Ghana Music Awards. Now, the two have added a beautiful new chapter to their story, bringing their families, friends and two cultures together in Accra. Efya and Tomi Thomas in black and olive-green outfits for their wedding reception. Photo Credit: Photo Humor/Instagram One of the lovely fashion moments from the celebration was their Nigerian traditional attire. The couple coordinated in rich bronze-brown shades, with Tomi wearing a woven traditional robe, complete with a matching traditional cap. He accessorised with layered orange coral neck beads, matching wrist beads and black loafers, while carrying a circular feathered fan inscribed with “OGENEE”. Efya was every bit his match in a fitted, floor-length bronze-brown gown, with gold and silver beadwork covering the corset bodice and sheer sleeves. The structured peplum details at the hips added shape to the dress, while a beaded treble clef motif on the skirt made a sweet reference to the music that brought so much of their story together. She finished with a pleated gold-and-bronze headwrap, a white-and-coral beaded choker, coral earrings and gold strappy heels. Tomi Thomas and Efya in coordinated bronze-brown traditional attire for their wedding in Accra. Photo Credit: Tomi Thomas/Instagram For their white wedding, the couple opted for a timeless black-and-white palette. Tomi kept things classic in a double-breasted white tuxedo jacket, complete with a white pocket square, crisp dress shirt and black bow tie. Black tailored trousers and matching dress shoes completed his look. Efya, meanwhile, made a beautiful bridal entrance in a fitted white lace mermaid gown with an embellished illusion neckline, sheer floral lace long sleeves and a corset-style waist. The voluminous detachable overskirt added another dimension to the dress, while her sleek low bun and large white structured bouquet with a jewelled centre completed her bridal look. item.title: UK MPs want AI watchdog with power to pull the plug on dangerous models
item.description: UK MPs want a watchdog with the power to pull the plug on dangerous AI models, rather than leave the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic to decide when they've gone too far. In a report shared with The Register ahead of publication on Wednesday, a parliamentary committee is calling for an AI Safety and Security Bill that would give a watchdog powers to intervene while models are still being developed. It could halt high-risk training and testing, block deployments, or suspend AI services if the risks can't be contained. LLMs are trained on billions of learned parameters and so developers can't always predict what a model will do in every situation. The recommendations come from Parliament's Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee, which questioned researchers, former AI employees, and representatives from OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, and Meta. All four companies assured MPs they wouldn't release models they considered unsafe. The trouble is, they don't use the same yardstick for safety, and UK law doesn't generally require them to get an independent opinion before releasing anything. "We cannot give today’s AI leaders unfettered freedom to behave like modern-day Dr Frankensteins, creating dangers beyond anyone’s control," said committee chair Liam Byrne MP. Just as with aviation, pharma or nuclear safety, UK government want to rely on manufacturers' assurance alone, and want regulation. "Our hearings exposed gaps in independent scrutiny, incident reporting and powers to stop unsafe systems. Once some models are released, they cannot reliably be recalled," added Byrne. "Protection must begin while systems are being built and tested." The committee's report, Guardrails for Growth: Making AI Safe, identifies ten holes in Britain's approach to AI safety, including the lack of mandatory incident reporting, limited access for independent testers, and inadequate protections for whistleblowers. The UK already has an AI Security Institute (AISI), which has made a name for itself testing some of the world's most powerful models, but its work depends on voluntary cooperation, and it has no authority to stop a company releasing a model that raises safety concerns. MPs want AISI to continue its testing work while a separate regulator takes responsibility for enforcement. Developers of designated high-risk systems would have to provide evidence supporting their safety claims and give independent researchers access to examine them. Significant changes to a model's capabilities or safeguards would trigger further scrutiny. Former AI employees also told MPs that raising safety concerns can come at a price. Restrictive contracts, commercial pressures, and financial disincentives can all discourage staff from speaking out, the committee heard. MPs want stronger legal protections for whistleblowers and compulsory reporting of AI incidents and near misses. There's a fair bit of money riding on this, too. item.content:encoded: UK MPs want a watchdog with the power to pull the plug on dangerous AI models, rather than leave the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic to decide when they've gone too far. In a report shared with The Register ahead of publication on Wednesday, a parliamentary committee is calling for an AI Safety and Security Bill that would give a watchdog powers to intervene while models are still being developed. It could halt high-risk training and testing, block deployments, or suspend AI services if the risks can't be contained. LLMs are trained on billions of learned parameters and so developers can't always predict what a model will do in every situation. The recommendations come from Parliament's Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee, which questioned researchers, former AI employees, and representatives from OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, and Meta. All four companies assured MPs they wouldn't release models they considered unsafe. The trouble is, they don't use the same yardstick for safety, and UK law doesn't generally require them to get an independent opinion before releasing anything. "We cannot give today’s AI leaders unfettered freedom to behave like modern-day Dr Frankensteins, creating dangers beyond anyone’s control," said committee chair Liam Byrne MP. Just as with aviation, pharma or nuclear safety, UK government want to rely on manufacturers' assurance alone, and want regulation. "Our hearings exposed gaps in independent scrutiny, incident reporting and powers to stop unsafe systems. Once some models are released, they cannot reliably be recalled," added Byrne. "Protection must begin while systems are being built and tested." The committee's report, Guardrails for Growth: Making AI Safe, identifies ten holes in Britain's approach to AI safety, including the lack of mandatory incident reporting, limited access for independent testers, and inadequate protections for whistleblowers. The UK already has an AI Security Institute (AISI), which has made a name for itself testing some of the world's most powerful models, but its work depends on voluntary cooperation, and it has no authority to stop a company releasing a model that raises safety concerns. MPs want AISI to continue its testing work while a separate regulator takes responsibility for enforcement. Developers of designated high-risk systems would have to provide evidence supporting their safety claims and give independent researchers access to examine them. Significant changes to a model's capabilities or safeguards would trigger further scrutiny. Former AI employees also told MPs that raising safety concerns can come at a price. Restrictive contracts, commercial pressures, and financial disincentives can all discourage staff from speaking out, the committee heard. MPs want stronger legal protections for whistleblowers and compulsory reporting of AI incidents and near misses. There's a fair bit of money riding on this, too. Using OECD productivity estimates, the committee calculates that AI could leave Britain's economy up to £400 billion larger over the next decade. It also sees an opportunity for the UK to make money from independently testing AI models, building on the expertise already established at AISI. MPs argue that stronger safeguards could encourage businesses, particularly smaller firms, to adopt the technology. "AI firms must be required to substantiate their safety claims, independent experts must be able to scrutinize them, and a regulator must have the power to intervene when risks cannot be controlled," Byrne said. "Ministers, accountable to Parliament, must decide what risks the public should be asked to bear." MPs want the new laws on the books in the next parliamentary session, and say Britain should use its turn at the G20 helm in 2027 to get other countries on board with tougher rules for AI testing, incident reporting, and risky model releases. Whether ministers are prepared to hand a watchdog the power to stop AI development is another matter. The committee's recommendations aren't binding, and the government has yet to commit to the proposed legislation. ®

item.title: Fifa’s World Cup TV rights documents indicate hydration breaks to stay in 2030
item.description: Controversial breaks were financial boon for broadcasters Fifa flags possible benefits but says no decision made Fifa’s tender documents for TV rights for the 2030 World Cup include a provision for broadcasters to sell adverts during hydration breaks in a strong indication the controversial ­stoppages will be retained. A three-minute break midway through each half was introduced for the first time at all 104 matches at last summer’s World Cup in the interests of player welfare, a radical move that also provided a commercial boon for broadcasters, particularly the rights holders in the United States, Fox Sports and Telemundo. Continue reading...

item.title: Detty December 2026 Travel Guide: Hotels, Resorts and Things to Do in Lagos and Enugu
item.description: December in Nigeria is practically a season of its own. Group chats are buzzing, flights are being booked, wedding invitations are coming in, an everyone seems to have holiday plans. From concerts, parties, and social gatherings to family reunions and Christmas celebrations, there is always something happening. For many, it is the most anticipated time of the year, a chance to reconnect with loved ones, explore new places, and make the most of the holidays. For some, it’s the excitement of Detty December in Lagos. For others, it’s finally getting everyone together for Christmas, taking a much-needed break, or planning a getaway after a long year. With so much happening, one thing deserves a little more attention than it usually gets: where you’ll be staying. A good hotel can make all the difference to your holiday. Think relaxing mornings, comfortable rooms, good food, a convenient location, exciting experiences nearby, and somewhere to unwind after a long day of activities. After all, where you stay can shape your entire holiday experience. Whether you’re planning to experience Detty December in Lagos or spend Christmas in Enugu, we’ve put together a guide to some accommodation options and experiences worth considering as you plan your holiday. Where to Stay in Lagos for Detty December Anyone who has experienced Lagos in December knows that the city takes the festive season seriously. Concerts, weddings, parties, restaurant dates, beach outings, family gatherings and the occasional last-minute plan that turns into the highlight of your holiday, there’s always something happening. With so much going on across the city, staying in a convenient location can save you time and make getting around much easier. Victoria Island remains one of Lagos’s most popular areas for visitors during the festive season, thanks to its restaurants, entertainment destinations, and proximity to major lifestyl attractions; it’s a top pick for visitors looking for the best of the city in December. A top hotel choice located in Landmark Lagos, Oniru, Victoria Island would be the Landmark Hotel, which offers an appealing option for visitors looking to enjoy the best of Lagos while having a comfortable place to retreat to at the end of the day. With ocean and city views, comfortable accommodation and access to the wider Landmark Lagos leisure and lifestyle ecosystem, Landmark Hotel gives guests more than just a place to stay. It puts them close to a range of experiences, dining options and entertainment destinations, making it easier to enjoy the festive season without having to travel too far. And the best part? There’s plenty to explore! Guests can enjoy dining experiences within the Landmark ecosystem, visit the Landmark Upside Down House, and attend events at POP Landmark, Landmark Center, or simply spend time exploring the recreational attractions available in the area. Victoria Island remains one of Lagos’s most popular areas for visitors during the festive season, thanks to its restaurants, entertainment destinations, and proximity to major lifestyl attractions; it’s a top pick for visitors looking for the best of the city in December. A top hotel choice located in Landmark Lagos, Oniru, Victoria Island would be the Landmark Hotel, which offers an appealing option for visitors looking to enjoy the best of Lagos while having a comfortable place to retreat to at the end of the day. With ocean and city views, comfortable accommodation and access to the wider Landmark Lagos leisure and lifestyle ecosystem, Landmark Hotel gives guests more than just a place to stay. It puts them close to a range of experiences, dining options and entertainment destinations, making it easier to enjoy the festive season without having to travel too far. And the best part? There’s plenty to explore! Guests can enjoy dining experiences within the Landmark ecosystem, visit the Landmark Upside Down House, and attend events at POP Landmark, Landmark Center, or simply spend time exploring the recreational attractions available in the area. Families visiting with children can also plan outings to the Landmark Kids Club. For visitors coming into Lagos for the holidays, having accommodation close to restaurants and recreational activities can make planning and commuting much easier. Planning a Christmas Getaway in Enugu? Consider a Lakeside Resort December isn’t only about the parties. It’s also one of the few times of the year when families get to spend uninterrupted time together, old friends reconnect, and people finally have an excuse to take that holiday they’ve been postponing. For many people from Eastern Nigeria, including those living abroad, returning home to celebrate Christmas with family and loved ones is a cherished annual tradition. If you’re planning a festive getaway this December, Enugu is one destination worth considering. Located in southeastern Nigeria, Enugu is the capital of Enugu State and is popularly known as the Coal City, a name rooted in its historic coal-mining industry. Beyond its history, the city is known for its scenic hills, rich Igbo cultural heritage, traditional cuisine, and vibrant hospitality and entertainment scene. There is also plenty to explore in and around the city. Visitors can enjoy panoramic views from Milliken Hill, discover the picturesque Ngwo Pine Forest and Waterfall, experience the natural beauty of Awhum Waterfall , or explore Nigeria’s cultural heritage at the National Museum of Unity. And for those looking to enjoy the city’s attractions while having a peaceful place to relax and reconnect with loved ones, a lakeside getaway offers the perfect opportunity to relax, unwind, and reconnect with loved ones. At Landmark Nike Lake Resort, the surroundings are part of the experience. The resort, which boasts over 200 rooms and 8 villas, is situated along the scenic shores of Nike Lake, offering a peaceful setting with lush greenery, lake views, comfortable accommodation, and recreational activities. It’s the kind of place where a morning can begin with breakfast overlooking the scenery, followed by a boat ride, an afternoon by the pool, or some outdoor adventure. For guests who enjoy a little adventure during their stay, there’s plenty to keep them entertained. From quad biking and recreational sports to a visit to the first Upside Down House in the Southeast, there’s something different to make the holiday even more memorable. The resort also offers dining options and spaces suited to gatherings and celebrations, making it an interesting choice for Christmas holidays, family reunions, and group getaways. For anyone visiting Enugu during the festive season, Landmark Nike Lake Resort offers more than just a place to stay. It’s an opportunity to slow down, enjoy the beauty of Nike Lake, spend quality time with family and friends, and create new memories along the way. And sometimes, that’s exactly what a holiday should be about. Tips for Choosing the Right Hotel or Resort This December December gets busy across Nigeria, and the last thing you want is the wrong accommodation. Before you book, here are four tips to help you get your holiday stay right; 1. Choose a Location That Works for Your Itinerary Consider the places you intend to visit and the activities on your holiday calendar. If you’re attending concerts, events, or spending most of your time around Victoria Island, staying within the area can help you save valuable time navigating Lagos traffic. For a more relaxed holiday, consider a resort that offers accommodation and recreational experiences within the same location. 2. Consider Who You’re Travelling With Your ideal accommodation will depend on the kind of trip you’re planning. Families travelling with children may prefer resorts with adjoining rooms, swimming pools, outdoor activities, and family-friendly attractions, while couples or solo travellers might prioritise comfortable rooms, dining experiences, and convenient access to entertainment. 3. Check the Facilities and What’s Included in Your Booking Before confirming your reservation, take a moment to find out what your accommodation package covers. Check for amenities such as breakfast, Wi-Fi, parking, recreational facilities, and on-site dining. If you’re booking a resort, confirm which activities are complimentary and which attract additional charges. This will help you plan your budget and avoid unexpected expenses during your stay. 4. Book Early and Confirm Your Reservation Details Hotels and resorts often experience increased demand during Christmas and New Year celebrations. Booking ahead gives you a better chance of securing your preferred room type and travel dates. Before making payment, confirm the room rates, check-in and check-out times, cancellation policy, and any festive-season offers or restrictions. Make the Most of Your December Holiday in Nigeria The festive season may last only a few weeks, but the best experiences have a way of staying with us long after the celebrations end. item.title: Tochukwu Ekoh: What My Friend’s Passing Taught Me About Kindness
item.description: A thoughtful young woman sits in a relaxed pose in a serene bedroom, reflecting peacefully. Photo credit: Alex Green/Pexels. I lost someone recently, and since then, I have found myself revisiting little moments, conversations and encounters I probably would not have given much thought to otherwise. We weren’t particularly close , or I wouldn’t describe our relationship that way . We had reconnected after a long time and started seeing each other more often, especially after I resumed work following an accident I was involved in. He gradually became part of my daily routine. Whenever I went to work, he would come to pick me up from the office, and we would go home together. In many ways, he looked out for me and made sure I got home safely. We started talking more. We would discuss life, share experiences and occasionally open up about things happening in our individual lives. There was also an emotional dimension to our friendship. He was interested in me romantically, I realised, but I didn’t feel the same way. I tried to understand my feelings, but the truth was that I simply wasn’t in love with him. I couldn’t manufacture feelings that weren’t there. Then I heard that he passed away. My first reaction, strangely, was guilt. I began asking myself: Was I a good friend to him? Was I kind enough? Was I considerate? Did I treat him well? Could I have done something differently? I caught myself wondering whether I should have given him a chance . Perhaps I should have allowed him to love me. But then would I have done that out of genuine affection or simply out of pity? And would that have been fair to either of us? My understanding is that not returning someone’s romantic feelings does not mean we cannot offer them genuine friendship, kindness and compassion. I didn’t owe him romantic love, but I could have been a good friend. That has stayed with me. Beyond the guilt, there was another question I couldn’t get out of my head: Why did God allow us to reconnect? Why, after such a long time, did our paths have to cross again? Why did we have to start talking, sharing experiences and becoming familiar with each other again, only for him to die shortly afterwards? Why him? Why at that particular time? What was the reason for that reconnection, and why did it have to end this way? The timing of certain events leaves you with more questions than answers. What makes this loss even more difficult to comprehend is how it happened. I had been the one who suffered an accident, yet I survived and was gradually recovering. He wasn’t sick. He hadn’t been involved in an accident. He simply slipped and fell, sustained an injury, and bled out. His body was not discovered until three days later. Three days. The loneliness he must have experienced within those three days, the possibility that he needed someone, and the heartbreaking thought that nobody knew what had happened to him. I cannot fully comprehend it. It also made me confront something I had perhaps never

item.content:encoded: A thoughtful young woman sits in a relaxed pose in a serene bedroom, reflecting peacefully. Photo credit: Alex Green/Pexels. I lost someone recently, and since then, I have found myself revisiting little moments, conversations and encounters I probably would not have given much thought to otherwise. We weren’t particularly close , or I wouldn’t describe our relationship that way .
